teile.einleitung: Suddenly the calf tightens and turns rock hard, and it really hurts. That is a **muscle cramp**. Usually it is harmless and goes away again after a short time.
wichtigste: A muscle cramp is a sudden, painful hardening of a muscle.
The calf cramps most often, frequently at night or during sport.
Gentle stretching usually helps at once.
With a calf cramp you pull the tip of the foot towards the shin.
Tiredness and a lot of sweating make cramps more likely.
An ordinary cramp lasts seconds to a few minutes.
If cramps occur very often, you should have them checked.

abschnitte.text: In a **muscle cramp** a muscle contracts **involuntarily**, that is, without you wanting it to. It then stays painfully hard and cannot simply be relaxed. An ordinary cramp is very painful but usually goes away after **seconds to a few minutes**. Afterwards the muscle can still hurt a little for a while. Occasional cramps are usually harmless.

abschnitte.titel: The calf as a cramp spot
abschnitte.text: The **calf muscles** cramp most often. Many people know night-time calf cramps that tear you out of sleep. They also often happen during sport, for example in football, swimming or long runs. Cramps are made more likely by **heavy tiredness** and by **a lot of sweating**. In this the body loses water and salts.

It helps best to **stretch** the cramping muscle **gently**. With a calf cramp you pull the **tip of the foot towards the shin**, for example with your hand or a towel. You can also stand up and press the heel into the floor. This stretches the calf, and the cramp eases. Afterwards a light massage often feels good.

Against cramps during sport it helps to **drink enough**, to **warm up** well and to stretch the muscles. Many people take magnesium for frequent cramps, but the effect is not reliably proven for ordinary cramps. If cramps occur very often or for no obvious reason, you should go to the **doctor**. There the cause can be checked.

gewusst: When swimming a cramp can be dangerous, so you should not swim far out alone.
Night-time calf cramps are more common in older people than in young ones.

teile.einleitung: In and on our body live countless micro-organisms, above all bacteria. All of them together are called the microbiome. Especially many live in the gut, where they help with digestion and influence our health.
wichtigste: Most bacteria live in the large intestine.
When they break down fibre, they make short-chain fatty acids.
Butyrate is the most important source of energy for the cells of the large intestine.
The groups Firmicutes and Bacteroidetes usually dominate.
A disturbed balance is called dysbiosis.
Prebiotics specifically promote useful gut bacteria.
Bacterial cells and body cells are roughly in the ratio 1 to 1.

abschnitte.text: The **microbiome** includes all the micro-organisms that live in and on the body: bacteria, but also fungi and viruses. They settle on the skin, in the mouth and above all in the **gut**. Most live in the **large intestine**. It used to be said that we have ten times more bacteria than body cells. According to more recent estimates, however, the ratio is about **1 to 1**.

Some parts of food our body cannot digest itself, for example much of the **fibre** from vegetables and wholegrain. The gut bacteria break them down. In doing so, **short-chain fatty acids** are made. The most important of them is **butyrate**, also called butyric acid. It is the most important **source of energy** for the cells of the wall of the large intestine. Some bacteria also make vitamins, such as vitamin K.

In healthy adults, two large groups of bacteria usually dominate: the **Firmicutes** and the **Bacteroidetes**. But the microbiome is slightly different in every person. If the balance is disturbed, this is called **dysbiosis**. This can happen, for example, after treatment with antibiotics. Researchers are investigating how dysbiosis is connected with various diseases.

A varied diet with plenty of fibre is good for the gut bacteria. **Prebiotics** are indigestible parts of food that specifically promote useful bacteria. They are found, for example, in onions, leeks or bananas. **Probiotics**, on the other hand, are living bacteria, for example in some yoghurts. How well their effect has been shown differs from product to product.

An unusual treatment is **stool transplantation**. In this, prepared stool from a healthy donor is put into the gut of a sick person. This gives them a healthy microbiome. It is used with **great success** for a **recurring infection with Clostridioides difficile**. After antibiotics, this bacterium can spread strongly in the gut and cause severe diarrhoea.

gewusst: The bacteria in a person’s gut weigh only about 200 grams all together, according to estimates.
Hundreds of different species of bacteria live in the gut.

teile.einleitung: A mosquito bite is annoying: it turns red, swells up and itches. Behind it is a mosquito that wanted to drink some of our blood.
wichtigste: Only the female mosquitoes bite.
They need blood so that their eggs can grow.
The mosquito bites with a thin proboscis.
The mosquito’s saliva makes the skin itch.
Mosquitoes find us through our breath and body smell.
Cooling helps against the itching, and scratching makes it worse.
A mosquito net protects at night.

abschnitte.text: Among mosquitoes, **only the females** bite. They need the blood so that their **eggs** can grow. The males feed on plant sap and nectar. The mosquito bites with its **proboscis**, a very thin snout on its head. With it she pierces the skin and sucks blood.

Mosquitoes have fine senses. They smell the **air we breathe out**, especially the carbon dioxide in it, and our **body smell**. Warmth also attracts them. In this way they find us even in the dark. Many mosquitoes are out and about in the **evening and at night**. That is why you often hear their buzzing just as you are falling asleep.

When biting, the mosquito puts a little **saliva** into the skin. It makes sure that the blood does not clot so quickly. Our body recognises the foreign substance and defends itself. In doing so the substance **histamine** is released. The spot turns into a small **red swelling** and itches.

Against the itching it helps to **cool** the spot, for example with a cold flannel. There are also ointments from the chemist. **Scratching** makes the itching stronger, and germs can get into the skin. You can prevent bites with long clothes, mosquito repellents and a **mosquito net** over the bed. Fly screens at the window also keep mosquitoes outside.

Mosquitoes lay their eggs **on or near water**, for example in ponds, puddles or water butts. The **larvae** live in the water until they become fully grown mosquitoes. Anyone who covers or regularly empties standing water in the garden has fewer mosquitoes. In Switzerland the **Asian tiger mosquito** has also been spreading for some years, at first mainly in Ticino.

gewusst: Mosquitoes beat their wings several hundred times a second, hence the high buzzing.
In warm countries mosquitoes can pass on diseases such as malaria.

teile.einleitung: Laughing, being amazed, frowning: we manage all of this with the **muscles of facial expression**. These facial muscles are special because they pull on the skin and so form our facial expression.
wichtigste: The muscles of facial expression form our facial expression.
Many of them attach to the skin and not to a bone.
They are controlled by the facial nerve, the seventh cranial nerve.
The ring muscle of the eye closes the eyelids.
The zygomaticus major muscle lifts the corners of the mouth when you smile.
The frontalis muscle lifts the eyebrows, and the corrugator muscle draws them together.
The buccinator muscle in the cheek and the platysma in the neck also belong to them.

abschnitte.titel: Muscles that pull on the skin
abschnitte.text: Most skeletal muscles connect two bones and so move a joint. With the **muscles of facial expression** it is different: they run from a bone or from connective tissue to the **skin**. When such a muscle contracts, the skin of the face moves with it. This is how smiles, wrinkles and grimaces arise. With our face we show joy, anger, fear or amazement, often without saying a word.

The eye is surrounded by a circular muscle, the **ring muscle of the eye** (orbicularis oculi muscle). It closes the eyelids when blinking and when squeezing the eyes shut. Above the eyes lies the **frontalis muscle**. It lifts the eyebrows and puts crosswise wrinkles in the forehead, for example when we are amazed. The **corrugator muscle** pulls the brows inwards and downwards. This makes the vertical wrinkles above the nose that you see when thinking or when annoyed.

Around the mouth lie especially many muscles of facial expression. The **zygomaticus major muscle** runs from the cheekbone to the corner of the mouth and lifts it up and outwards when you smile. The **buccinator muscle** lies in the cheek. It presses air out of the mouth and is therefore also called the trumpeter’s muscle. When chewing it helps to hold the food between the teeth. In the neck lies the **platysma**, a thin, flat skin muscle that pulls the corners of the mouth down and tightens the skin of the neck.

All the muscles of facial expression are controlled by the **facial nerve** (nervus facialis). It is the seventh of twelve cranial nerves and branches out like a fan across the face. If this nerve is paralysed, it is called **facial palsy**. One half of the face then droops, the eye is hard to close and the corner of the mouth sinks. Often such a paralysis improves again with time.

gewusst: A real, happy smile can be recognised by the ring muscle of the eye also working and little laughter lines appearing.
The naturalist Charles Darwin wrote a book as early as 1872 on the expression of feelings in humans and animals.

teile.einleitung: Melanin is a natural pigment in the body. It gives the skin, hair and eyes their colour. It also protects the skin from the rays of the sun.
wichtigste: Melanin is a pigment of the skin.
It is made by cells called melanocytes.
It protects the skin from UV radiation.
When you get a tan, the skin makes more melanin.
Dark and light skin differ mainly in the amount and kind of melanin.
Melanin is also found in hair and in the iris.
In albinism the body makes hardly any melanin or none.

abschnitte.text: **Melanin** is a dark **pigment** that the body makes itself. It is made by special cells in the outer layer of the skin, the **melanocytes**. They pass the melanin on to the surrounding skin cells. There are different kinds of melanin: a brownish black one and a reddish yellow one. Depending on the mixture, many different shades arise.

The **UV radiation** of the sun can damage the skin cells. Melanin absorbs part of this radiation and so protects the skin. When we are in the sun, the skin makes **more melanin**: we get **brown**. This tan is therefore a protective reaction. But it is not enough, so you still need sunscreen, a hat and shade.

People have very different **skin colours**. This is mainly because of the **amount and kind of melanin**, not the number of melanocytes. People whose ancestors lived in sunny regions usually have darker skin, which protects well against UV radiation. In regions with little sun, the skin is often lighter. It can then make vitamin D better, for which some sunlight is needed.

Melanin is found not only in the skin. It also colours the **hair** and the **iris** of the eyes. A lot of melanin gives brown eyes and dark hair. When no more melanin is made in the hair in old age, it turns grey or white. In **albinism** the body makes hardly any melanin or none from birth. People affected have very pale skin and hair and are sensitive to the sun.

A dangerous skin cancer can arise from the pigment cells, **malignant melanoma**. An important risk factor is sunburn, especially in childhood. That is why good sun protection is important. Anyone who has a mole that changes should have it looked at by a doctor.

gewusst: The dark ink of cuttlefish also contains melanin.
Freckles are small patches in which the skin makes more melanin.

teile.einleitung: Migraine is a special form of headache that comes in attacks. The pain is often very severe and comes with other symptoms. Many people are affected, including children and teenagers.
wichtigste: Migraine pain is typically throbbing and often on one side.
Nausea and sensitivity to light often come with it.
Sometimes an aura with disturbed vision comes first.
An untreated attack lasts 4 to 72 hours in adults.
In adulthood women are more often affected.
Rest in a darkened room helps many people.
A headache diary helps to recognise triggers.

abschnitte.text: The word **migraine** comes from the Greek word for **“half the skull”**. It describes that the pain often affects only **one side of the head**. A **throbbing**, pounding pain is typical. It often gets worse with movement. According to the technical definition, an untreated attack in adults lasts **4 to 72 hours**. In children the attacks are often shorter.

Other symptoms often go with migraine. Many people affected have **nausea** and sometimes have to be sick. They are **sensitive to light** and often to noise too. In some people an **aura** comes before the headache. In it you see, for example, **flickering** or **zigzag lines**. The aura usually lasts less than an hour.

Migraine is widespread. In **adulthood**, **women** are affected clearly more often than men. In children the difference is smaller. Often other family members have migraine too. More common than migraine is the **tension headache**. It usually feels **pressing**, like a tight band, and affects **both sides** of the head.

Migraine can be made more likely by various **triggers**. These include stress, too little sleep, skipped meals or not drinking enough. These triggers are different in every person. A **headache diary** helps to recognise them. In it you write down when the pain comes, how strong it is and what you did beforehand.

During an attack, **rest in a darkened room** helps many people. Sleep can also end the attack. There are also **painkillers** and special migraine medicines that you take after medical advice. Anyone who has attacks often can talk to a doctor about preventive treatment. A regular daily routine and exercise also help.

gewusst: The World Health Organization counts migraine among the diseases that cause the most years of impaired health worldwide.
Some children have a form in which stomach pains mainly occur instead of headaches.

teile.einleitung: Melanoma is a malignant skin cancer that arises from the pigment cells of the skin. It is also called black skin cancer. If it is recognised early, it can usually be cured well.
wichtigste: Many moles and sunburns in childhood clearly raise the risk.
The ABCDE rule helps to recognise suspicious moles.
The “E” stands for evolution or change.
In fair-skinned people, superficial spreading melanoma is the most common.
For the outlook, the tumour thickness according to Breslow is especially important.
About half of skin melanomas carry a BRAF mutation.
Immune checkpoint inhibitors have greatly improved treatment.

abschnitte.titel: How it arises and the risk
abschnitte.text: A **melanoma** arises from the **melanocytes**, the pigment cells of the skin. An important trigger is the **UV radiation** of the sun. The risk rises especially clearly in people with **many moles** and with **sunburns in childhood**. Fair skin and cases in the family also raise the risk. Switzerland is among the countries in Europe with especially many cases of melanoma.

With the **ABCDE rule** you can assess moles. **A** stands for asymmetry, that is, an uneven shape. **B** stands for a blurred border. **C** stands for colour, that is, several colours. **D** stands for a diameter of more than about 5 millimetres. **E** stands for **evolution or change**. If any of these applies, you should have the mole checked by a doctor.

In fair-skinned people the **superficial spreading melanoma** is the most common. It first grows flat and wide. The **nodular melanoma**, on the other hand, grows **deep as a lump** from the start. The **acral lentiginous melanoma** often appears on the **palms**, the **soles of the feet** or **under the nails**. In about half of skin melanomas, a change is found in the gene **BRAF**.

A suspicious mole is cut out and examined in the laboratory. For the **outlook**, the **tumour thickness according to Breslow** is especially important. It shows how deep the tumour has grown into the skin. The thinner it is, the better the chances of a cure. In thicker melanomas, the **sentinel lymph node** is often examined. This is used to check whether tumour cells have spread into the **lymph channels**.

In the past, melanomas with secondary growths in other organs were hard to treat. Since the **2010s** this has greatly improved. **Immune checkpoint inhibitors** release a brake on the immune system, so that it can attack the cancer cells better. In a BRAF mutation there are also medicines that act specifically against this change. But the most important thing is still protection from sunburn.

gewusst: For developing the immune checkpoint inhibitors, James Allison and Tasuku Honjo received the Nobel Prize in Medicine in 2018.
A melanoma can also arise in places that rarely get any sun, for example under a nail.

teile.einleitung: Mechanoreceptors are sensory cells that react to mechanical stimuli. These include pressure, touch, stretching and vibrations. Thanks to them we can feel by touch, hear and sense how our body is moving.
wichtigste: Mechanoreceptors react to pressure, touch and stretching.
Meissner’s corpuscles report fine, light touches.
Merkel cells report sustained pressure.
Ruffini endings report the stretching of the skin.
The hair cells in the inner ear are mechanoreceptors.
Ardem Patapoutian received the Nobel Prize in 2021 for discovering sensors for pressure and touch.

abschnitte.text: In our skin sit different **mechanoreceptors**. Each kind reports something different. **Meissner’s corpuscles** lie, for example, in the fingertips and report **fine, light touches**. **Merkel cells** report **sustained pressure**, for example when we hold a pen tight. **Ruffini endings** report how strongly the skin is **stretched**, for example when bending the fingers.

The fine **hairs** on the skin also help us to feel. At their roots sit sensory cells. If a hair moves even a little, they report it to the brain at once. That is why you can feel a **mosquito** on your arm even when it hardly touches the skin. The hairs work like little levers.

Mechanoreceptors are found not only in the skin. In the **inner ear** sit the **hair cells**. They carry fine projections that are bent by sound waves or movements. Nerve signals arise from this. This is how we can **hear** and keep our **balance**. Other mechanoreceptors in muscles and tendons report how much they are stretched.

Many animals have especially fine senses of touch. **Cats** use their long **whiskers** to pick up even the finest movements of air, and so find their way around even in the dark. **Fish** sense movements of water and currents with the **lateral line organ**. It runs as a line along both sides of their body. In this way they notice obstacles and other animals.

For a long time it was not known exactly how a cell turns pressure into an electrical signal. The scientist **Ardem Patapoutian** discovered special proteins in the cell membrane for this that serve as **sensors for pressure and touch**. They are called **Piezo channels**. For this he received the **Nobel Prize in Medicine** in **2021**, together with David Julius, who studied sensors for heat.

gewusst: In the fingertips lie particularly many touch receptors, which is why they are so sensitive.
People who read Braille feel tiny dots with their fingertips.

teile.einleitung: **Bullying** means that someone is tormented, left out or shown up again and again over a longer time. It can happen at school, in a club, at work or online. What matters is this: nobody has to put up with it alone, and everybody can help.
wichtigste: Bullying means that someone is repeatedly harassed over a longer time.
Bullying through phones, chats and social networks is called cyberbullying.
Bystanders can stop bullying if they step in or fetch help.
With cyberbullying you should save evidence and tell adults.
Bullying can lead to fear, stomach aches and withdrawal.
Pro Juventute gives advice around the clock on the number 147.
Dan Olweus was one of the first to research bullying at schools.

abschnitte.text: In **bullying**, a person is not just teased once, but again and again over a longer time. This can happen through insults, laughing at them, rumours, leaving them out or taking their things. Often several people are against one person who can hardly defend themselves alone. The German word “Mobbing” comes from the English “to mob”, which means roughly to attack as a crowd. The term originally comes from **behavioural research** on animals.

In **cyberbullying**, people are insulted, shown up or threatened through phones, chats and social networks. It can go on around the clock and reach very many people. Anyone affected should **save evidence**, for example with screenshots. After that you tell parents, teachers or other people you trust. The bullies can be **blocked and reported**.

In bullying there are often many **bystanders**. Anyone who watches and stays silent often encourages the bullies, even without meaning to. Anyone who stands by the person affected or **fetches help** can achieve a lot. Schools help with a good protection plan: **clear class rules**, fixed contact people and quick action. The whole school community is called upon.

Bullying hurts, even when you cannot see it from outside. People affected often have **fear**, stomach aches or sleep problems and withdraw. That is why early help is important. In Switzerland, **Pro Juventute** offers children and young people advice around the clock on the number **147**. The service is confidential and free, also by chat or email.

From the 1970s on, the psychologist **Dan Olweus** investigated violence among pupils in Norway and Sweden. He developed a well-known **prevention programme** against bullying at schools. In the 1980s the occupational psychologist **Heinz Leymann**, who worked in Sweden, made the term known for harassment at the workplace. Since then people also speak of bullying among adults.

gewusst: The 147 advice line from Pro Juventute does not appear on the phone bill.
Studies show that bullying often stops when classmates clearly stand up against it.

teile.einleitung: In the stomach our food is not only collected but also treated chemically. Stomach acid plays an important part in this. It is very strong and helps with digestion and with protection from germs.
wichtigste: Stomach acid consists mainly of hydrochloric acid.
In an empty stomach the pH value is about 1 to 2.
The acid is made by the parietal cells of the stomach lining.
It kills many germs from food.
A thick layer of mucus protects the stomach wall from its own acid.
The acid activates the protein-splitting enzyme pepsin.
An adult makes about 2 to 3 litres of gastric juice a day.

abschnitte.text: Gastric juice contains **hydrochloric acid**. This acid is so strong that the pH value in an empty stomach is about **1 to 2**. The **pH value** shows how acid something is: 7 is neutral, and the smaller the number, the more acid. For comparison: lemon juice has a pH value of about 2. After eating, the contents of the stomach become somewhat less acid, because the food buffers part of the acid.

The inner wall of the stomach is lined with the **stomach lining**. In it lie many small glands. In these glands sit the **parietal cells**, which make the acid and release it into the inside of the stomach. Other cells make mucus or early forms of enzymes. Together they produce about **2 to 3 litres of gastric juice** a day.

The acid changes the **proteins** from food. It destroys their three-dimensional shape, and the proteins are said to be **denatured**. Unfolded proteins are easier to break down. The acid also turns the inactive early form **pepsinogen** into the active enzyme **pepsin**. Pepsin splits the proteins into smaller pieces, which are digested further later in the intestine.

abschnitte.titel: Protection from germs and protection of the stomach wall
abschnitte.text: With food, **bacteria** and other germs often get into the body. Many of them do not survive the strong acid. This is how the stomach protects against germs. But why does the stomach not digest itself? The lining makes a thick **layer of mucus** that keeps the acid away from the cells. In addition the cells of the lining renew themselves very quickly.

The stomach begins its work even before we eat. When we **smell** food, see it or just think about it, **nerves** send signals to the stomach. It then starts making gastric juice. When food arrives in the stomach, the production is stimulated even more. In this way the stomach is well prepared for the meal.

gewusst: Hydrochloric acid is so strong that it is also used in industry for cleaning metal.
The cells of the stomach lining are completely replaced within a few days.
Acid belching is called heartburn: in it, stomach acid gets into the gullet.

teile.einleitung: Sometimes your tummy rumbles loudly, especially when you are hungry. This is called stomach rumbling. It is quite normal and shows that the stomach and intestines are working.
wichtigste: When you are hungry, you often hear your stomach rumble.
The noise is made when air and digestive juice are pushed along.
The noises from the belly are also called bowel sounds.
Stomach rumbling is not dangerous but normal.
The belly can also rumble after eating, while digesting.
A doctor can hear the sounds well with a stethoscope.

abschnitte.text: The stomach and intestines are surrounded by **muscles**. These tighten again and again and push the contents along. In doing so, **air and digestive juice** are pushed to and fro. This makes noises, a **rumbling** or gurgling. When the stomach is empty, there is little food to muffle the sound. That is why it then sounds especially loud.

When you have not eaten for some time, the stomach and intestines clear themselves out with strong movements. That is why the stomach often rumbles when you are **hungry**. **Eating something** usually helps against this. But the belly can also rumble **after eating**, because then it is **digesting** and pushing the food pulp along. The belly is never really completely silent.

The noises from the belly are also called **bowel sounds**. Stomach rumbling is **not dangerous**, but a sign that digestion is working. A doctor can hear the noises well with a **stethoscope**. In this way they find out whether the intestine is moving normally. You do not have to be embarrassed by rumbling: it happens to all people and to many animals too.

gewusst: The technical word for the belly noises is “borborygmus”, which is meant to imitate the sound.
A large part of the rumbling does not come from the stomach at all, but from the intestine.

teile.einleitung: The rectum is the last section of the intestine. This is where stools are collected until we go to the toilet. It works closely with the sphincter muscles at the anus.
wichtigste: The rectum is the last part of the intestine before the anus.
Its technical name is the rectum.
It collects the stools until they are emptied.
In an adult it is about 15 centimetres long.
It lies in the pelvis.
Directly before it lies the S-shaped sigmoid colon.

abschnitte.text: The **rectum** belongs to the **large intestine** and is its last section. It lies in the **pelvis**, in front of the sacrum. Directly before the rectum lies an S-shaped bent part of the large intestine, the **sigmoid colon**. At the end of the rectum comes the anal canal with the **anus**. In an adult the rectum is about **15 centimetres** long.

In the large intestine, a lot of water is taken from the food pulp. This is how **stools** are made. The rectum serves as a **store**: this is where the stools collect until we pass them. Its wall can stretch, so that it can take in a certain amount. This means we do not have to go to the toilet all the time.

abschnitte.titel: The urge to go to the toilet
abschnitte.text: When the rectum fills, its wall is **stretched**. Sensory cells in the wall report this to the brain. We then feel the **urge** to go to the toilet. At the anus there are two **sphincter muscles**. The inner one works by itself. The **outer sphincter** we can control **at will**. This way we can wait until we reach a toilet.

For good digestion, **fibre** from vegetables, fruit and wholegrain foods helps. Drinking enough and exercise are also important. You should not hold back the urge to go to the toilet for a long time too often. Anyone who notices blood in their stools or has complaints for a long time should see a doctor. From a certain age, a screening examination of the bowel is recommended in Switzerland.

gewusst: Small children learn only over time to control the outer sphincter consciously.
The word “rectum” comes from Latin and means “straight”, although the rectum is slightly curved.

teile.einleitung: Why do we study for an exam, train for a race or practise an instrument? Behind it lies **motivation**, the force that drives us to pursue a goal. It can come from within or from outside.
wichtigste: Intrinsic motivation arises from enjoyment of the activity itself.
Extrinsic motivation comes from outside, for example through marks, money or praise.
The messenger substance dopamine plays an important part in the brain’s reward system.
The hierarchy of needs is named after Abraham Maslow.
Clear, achievable goals motivate best.
Putting tasks off is called procrastination.
In flow you become completely absorbed in an activity.

abschnitte.text: Experts distinguish two kinds of motivation. **Intrinsic** means “from within”: you do something because it is fun or interesting, for example reading a book or playing football. **Extrinsic** means “from outside”: you are driven by reward or punishment, for example through marks, money or praise. Often both work together. Interesting is the **overjustification effect**: if you reward someone for something they enjoy anyway, their inner enjoyment of it can fall.

In the brain there is a **reward system**. The messenger substance **dopamine** plays an important part in it. It is released when we expect a reward. Dopamine drives us to pursue a goal and to keep going. That is why it feels good when we come closer to a goal.

The psychologist **Abraham Maslow** arranged human needs in levels that build on each other. At the very bottom are **basic bodily needs** such as eating, drinking and sleeping. These are followed by safety, belonging, recognition and finally self-fulfilment. Only when the lower needs are met do higher ones come to the fore. The picture of it as a pyramid was made known later by others.

**Clear, achievable goals** motivate best. They show what is to be done, and anyone who manages small stages keeps going. But many people also know the opposite: important tasks are put off again and again until later. This is called **procrastination**. It helps to divide a big task into small steps and simply to start with the first one.

Sometimes you are so absorbed in an activity that you forget the time. The psychologist **Mihály Csíkszentmihályi** called this state **flow**. It arises when a task is neither too easy nor too hard. If it is too easy it becomes boring, and if it is too hard stress results. Many people experience flow in sport, playing music, drawing or playing games.

gewusst: The word motivation comes from the Latin “movere”, which means to move.
Even looking forward to a reward makes the brain release dopamine.

teile.einleitung: Anyone who works or plays a lot on the computer moves their hand and arm in the same way, often for hours. This can cause pains that are called mouse arm in everyday language. You can prevent it with simple measures.
wichtigste: The technical name is repetitive strain injury, or RSI for short.
The cause is many small, uniform movements with a rigid posture.
Typical signs are pain, tingling and loss of strength in the hand, arm or shoulder.
Regular short breaks and variety help to prevent it.
A vertical mouse keeps the forearm in a natural position.
Related complaints are tendon sheath inflammation, carpal tunnel syndrome and tennis elbow.

abschnitte.text: **Mouse arm** is not an exact medical term but a name from everyday life. Experts speak of **repetitive strain injury**, or **RSI** for short. The main cause is **many small, uniform movements**, for example when clicking and typing. In addition there is often a **rigid posture** of the shoulders and neck over a long time.

At the beginning you often feel only a pulling or a tiredness in the arm. Later, **pain**, **tingling** and **loss of strength** in the hand, forearm, elbow or **shoulder** can be added. Sometimes the fingers feel numb. The complaints appear first at work, and later also at rest. That is why you should take early warning signs seriously.

Constantly repeated movements of the hand and fingers can cause **tendon sheath inflammation**. In **carpal tunnel syndrome** the median nerve is squeezed at the wrist. Then it is mainly the thumb, index finger and middle finger that tingle. In **tennis elbow**, the points where the tendons attach on the outer elbow are irritated. Despite the name, it can also arise from a lot of work with a mouse.

Most important are **regular short breaks** and **variety** in movements. In between you can shake out your hands, stretch your arms or stand up briefly. A well-arranged workplace helps: the screen is at eye level and the forearms rest loosely. A **vertical mouse** keeps the forearm in a natural **handshake position**. Keyboard shortcuts also replace many a mouse click.

gewusst: With an ordinary mouse the forearm is twisted, with a vertical mouse it is not.
Similar complaints can also arise from gaming or from a lot of typing on a phone.

teile.einleitung: Cancer can spread in the body. In this, cells break away from the original tumour and form new growths in other places. These are called metastases or secondary tumours.
wichtigste: A metastasis is a secondary tumour far from the original tumour.
The original tumour is called the primary tumour.
Cancer cells spread through lymph and blood vessels.
The first lymph node in the drainage area is called the sentinel lymph node.
Tumours of the bowel often spread first to the liver through the portal vein.
The seed and soil hypothesis of 1889 explains preferred target organs.
In most cancer patients, the effects of metastases are the real cause of death.

abschnitte.text: A tumour arises where cells begin to grow out of control. This first tumour is called the **primary tumour**. In malignant tumours, cells can break away and reach other places in the body. If they take root there, a **metastasis** arises, that is, a **secondary tumour far from the original tumour**. The word comes from Greek and means roughly “moving elsewhere”.

Cancer cells spread mainly by two routes: through the **lymph vessels** and through the **blood vessels**. To be able to travel, they have to detach from neighbouring cells. In the **epithelial-mesenchymal transition**, cells lose their cohesion and become mobile. Cancer cells that can be detected in the blood are called **circulating tumour cells**. They are looked for, for example, in a **liquid biopsy**, a blood test.

The lymph from the area of a tumour flows first to a particular lymph node. It is called the **sentinel lymph node**. In operations it is often removed on purpose and examined. If no cancer cells are found in it, spread through the lymph channel is less likely. In this way larger operations can sometimes be avoided.

Tumours do not spread at random, but preferably to certain organs. The English doctor Stephen Paget explained this in **1889** with the **seed and soil hypothesis**. The cancer cell is like a seed that only grows on suitable soil. Blood flow also plays a part: blood from the bowel flows through the **portal vein** first to the **liver**. That is why tumours of the bowel often form metastases there first.

In most cancer patients it is not the primary tumour but **the effects of metastases** that are the real cause of death. That is why it is so important to detect cancer early, before it spreads. Today, however, there are also treatments that can keep metastases in check for a long time. Research on metastases is therefore an important field of cancer medicine.

gewusst: A metastasis in the liver consists of cells from the original organ, for example bowel cells.
Not every cancer cell in the blood forms a metastasis, and most do not survive the journey.

teile.einleitung: The milk teeth are a child’s first teeth. They grow from about the age of six months and are gradually replaced by the permanent teeth from about the age of six. This is necessary because the jaw grows and later needs bigger and more teeth.
wichtigste: The milk teeth consist of 20 teeth.
The first milk tooth usually comes at about six to eight months.
At about two and a half to three years old, the set of milk teeth is complete.
From about the age of six, the milk teeth fall out and permanent teeth grow in.
The change of teeth is necessary because the jaw grows and needs bigger teeth.
The permanent set has 32 teeth including the wisdom teeth.
Milk teeth also have to be cleaned well so that they do not get decayed.

abschnitte.text: The **milk teeth** are the first set of teeth in humans and many mammals. They have 20 teeth, ten each at the top and bottom. In each half of the jaw there are two incisors, one canine and two molars. The name probably comes from the whitish colour of the teeth and from the fact that babies drink milk at this time.

Usually the lower middle incisors come first, at about six to eight months. **Teething** can hurt, and babies then dribble a lot and like to chew on everything. Gradually the other teeth follow. At about two and a half to three years old, the set of milk teeth is complete.

From about the age of six, the **change of teeth** begins. Under the milk teeth, the permanent teeth are already growing. They slowly dissolve the roots of the milk teeth until these wobble and fall out. Often the first to arrive is a big permanent molar right at the back, the six-year molar, without a milk tooth falling out for it.

A child’s jaw is small and has room only for small teeth. As you grow, the **jaw** becomes bigger too. The milk teeth would then be too small and too few, so they are replaced by bigger permanent teeth. The **permanent set** has 28 teeth, and with the four wisdom teeth it is 32.

Milk teeth also need good care, because they keep the space free for the permanent teeth. If a milk tooth falls out too early because of **tooth decay**, the new teeth can grow crooked. Brushing twice a day with children’s toothpaste and eating little sweet food protects the teeth. In Switzerland children visit the school dentist regularly, and there are lessons on tooth brushing at school.

begriffe.erklaerung: One of a child’s first 20 teeth.
All the teeth in the mouth together.
A hole in a tooth that is caused by bacteria and sugar.
The bone in which the teeth sit.

gewusst: In many countries children put their lost milk tooth under the pillow for the tooth fairy, and in Spain a mouse called Ratoncito Pérez fetches it.
Rarely, babies are born with a tooth already.
During the change of teeth the mouth is sometimes full of gaps for months, and that is quite normal.

teile.einleitung: With a microscope you can see things that are far too small for the naked eye. It magnifies tiny living things, cells or crystals. In many schools there are microscopes for research.
wichtigste: Glass lenses in the microscope magnify the image.
You look in through the eyepiece.
The sample lies on a small plate of glass, the slide.
Eyepiece times objective gives the total magnification.
You focus the image with the focus knob.
Antonie van Leeuwenhoek was one of the first to see bacteria, around 1676.

abschnitte.text: A microscope magnifies with **glass lenses**. At the top you look in through the **eyepiece**. At the bottom, close to the sample, sits the **objective lens**. The sample lies on a small plate of glass, the **slide**. It is placed on the **stage**. In a school microscope the **light** usually shines **from below** through the sample. That is why the samples must be very thin, so that light can shine through.

Both the eyepiece and the objective lens magnify. To work out the **total magnification**, you multiply the two numbers. If the eyepiece magnifies **10 times** and the objective lens also **10 times**, then the microscope magnifies **100 times**. Many microscopes have several objective lenses that you can switch between. A **magnifying glass** magnifies much less strongly than a microscope.

At first you often see only a blurred image. With the **focus knob** you change the distance between the sample and the objective lens. This brings the image **into focus**. It is best to start with the smallest magnification. After that you can choose a stronger objective lens and adjust with the fine focus.

abschnitte.titel: A world in a drop of water
abschnitte.text: Even a single drop of **pond water** is full of life. In the microscope you see **tiny living things**, for example slipper animalcules, algae or small crustaceans. An onion skin is also exciting: in it you can see the individual **cells** like little bricks. You can also look at hairs, grains of salt or leaves.

The Dutchman **Antonie van Leeuwenhoek** built his own, very good microscopes with only one lens in the 17th century. Around **1676** he was one of the first to see **bacteria** and other tiny living things. He called them “little animals”. Today there are also electron microscopes. They work not with light but with electrons and magnify even much more strongly.

gewusst: Van Leeuwenhoek was actually a cloth merchant and built his microscopes as a hobby.
The word “microscope” comes from Greek and means roughly “looking at small things”.

teile.einleitung: The maximum heart rate is the highest number of heartbeats per minute that a person can reach at greatest effort. In sport it helps to steer training correctly. You can estimate it roughly or measure it exactly.
wichtigste: A simple rule of thumb is: 220 minus your age.
For a 14-year-old this gives 206 beats per minute.
The maximum heart rate falls with age.
It is determined more precisely with an exercise test.
Easy basic training is at about 60 to 70 per cent.
You can feel the pulse well at the wrist.
A heart rate watch with a sensor measures the pulse continuously.

abschnitte.text: With every beat the **heart** pumps blood into the arteries. You can feel this pressure wave as the **pulse**. You can feel it well at the **wrist** on the thumb side or at the side of the neck. You count the beats for 15 seconds, for example, and multiply by 4. This gives the beats per minute. When you exert yourself, the heart beats faster, until it reaches the **maximum heart rate**.

A well-known rule of thumb is: **220 minus your age**. For a 14-year-old this gives 220 minus 14, that is **206** beats per minute. The formula also shows that the maximum heart rate **falls with age**. But it is only a rough guide. In many people the real value is clearly higher or lower.

The maximum heart rate is determined more precisely with an **exercise test**. In this you increase the effort step by step, for example on a treadmill or a bike, until you cannot go on. Such a test should only be done when healthy and best of all under guidance. In sport, a **heart rate watch with a sensor** measures the pulse continuously, either at the wrist or with a chest strap.

With the maximum heart rate you can work out **training zones**. Easy **basic training** is at about **60 to 70 per cent** of the maximum heart rate. In this you can still talk well. An example: if someone has a maximum heart rate of 200, 70 per cent of that is **140** beats per minute. Harder training is higher but is held only briefly.

gewusst: A trained heart often beats more slowly at rest than an untrained one.
The maximum heart rate can hardly be raised by training, but the resting heart rate can fall.

teile.einleitung: Malaria is a dangerous infectious disease that occurs in warm countries. It is caused by tiny parasites and passed on by mosquitoes. Every year very many people around the world fall ill with it.
wichtigste: Malaria is passed on by the Anopheles mosquito.
Only the females bite and pass on the disease.
Recurring attacks of fever are typical.
The germs multiply in the red blood cells.
Most cases occur in Africa south of the Sahara.
A mosquito net protects especially well at night.
World Malaria Day is on 25 April.

abschnitte.text: The name **malaria** comes from the Italian expression **“mala aria”**, which means **“bad air”**. In the past people believed that the disease was caused by the damp air in marshes. Today we know that tiny single-celled **parasites** cause the disease. They are called **plasmodia**. Many mosquitoes live in marshy areas, though, and so the old idea had a grain of truth.

Malaria is passed on by the **Anopheles mosquito**. **Only the females** bite, because they need blood to make eggs. When a mosquito bites a sick person, it takes in germs. At the next bite it can pass them on to another person. The mosquitoes bite mainly at dusk and at night.

The germs first get into the **liver**. After that they enter the **red blood cells** and multiply there. When the blood cells burst, new germs are set free. This leads to **recurring attacks of fever** with shivering and sweating. Without treatment malaria can become life-threatening, especially for small children.

Malaria occurs in tropical and subtropical regions. The **most cases** occur in **Africa south of the Sahara**. The disease does not occur in Switzerland. But travellers can catch it in malaria regions. That is why they get advice before the journey, for example at a travel medicine clinic. Every year on **25 April** it is **World Malaria Day**.

A simple and effective protection is a **mosquito net** over the bed, often treated with an insect repellent. Long clothes and mosquito repellent on the skin also help. An old drug against malaria is **quinine**. It comes from the bark of the **cinchona tree** from South America. Today there are other medicines and now also vaccines for children in malaria regions.

gewusst: Quinine gives tonic water its bitter taste.
The Chinese scientist Tu Youyou received the Nobel Prize in Medicine in 2015 for discovering the malaria drug artemisinin.
Because of diseases like malaria, mosquitoes are regarded as the most dangerous animals in the world for humans.

teile.einleitung: Phones, games and social media are fun and part of everyday life. But some people can hardly stop using them, even when it harms them. This is then called media addiction.
wichtigste: The WHO has included gaming disorder in the ICD-11.
One warning sign is when you neglect friends and school.
FOMO means the fear of missing out.
Bright screen light in the evening slows the sleep hormone melatonin.
Likes work through the messenger substance dopamine.
The Swiss JAMES study investigates how young people use media.
Charging your phone outside the bedroom helps you to sleep.

abschnitte.titel: When does it become an addiction?
abschnitte.text: Not every long time on the phone is an addiction. We speak of **media addiction** when someone loses control and carries on despite the disadvantages. **Warning signs** are, for example, when you **neglect friends and school**, give up hobbies or get irritable when you cannot be online. The World Health Organization **WHO** has included **gaming disorder** as a disease in its list **ICD-11**.

When we get a **like** or win something in a game, the brain releases the messenger substance **dopamine**. It belongs to the **reward system** and gives a good feeling. That is why we want more of it. Some apps are designed for exactly this. With **endless scrolling** the content never ends, and so you keep swiping on.

New terms have arisen around the phone. **FOMO** stands for “fear of missing out”, that is, the **fear of missing something**. It makes many people check constantly. **Phubbing** is when someone ignores the person in front of them and looks at their phone instead. The word is made up of “phone” and “snubbing”, which means ignoring someone rudely.

Screens give off bright, bluish light. In the evening it slows the making of the sleep hormone **melatonin**. You get tired later and sleep worse. In addition there are messages that wake you in the night. A simple help is to **charge your phone outside the bedroom** and to use no more screens for an hour before sleep.

The **JAMES study** has regularly investigated since 2010 how young people in Switzerland use media. It is carried out by ZHAW and Swisscom. Anyone who notices that their use of media is becoming a problem can talk to parents, teachers or school social work. Help is also available around the clock from the advice service of **Pro Juventute** on the number **147**.

gewusst: JAMES stands for “Jugend, Aktivitäten, Medien, Erhebung Schweiz”, which means Youth, Activities, Media, Survey Switzerland.
Many phones have a function that shows how long you have spent on the screen in a day.

teile.einleitung: When we lift an arm, an order has to pass from the nerve to the muscle. This happens at the **motor end plate**, a special point of contact between a nerve cell and a muscle fibre.
wichtigste: The motor end plate is the synapse between a motor neuron and a skeletal muscle fibre.
The messenger substance is acetylcholine.
An inflow of calcium into the nerve ending triggers its release.
In the muscle membrane sit nicotinic acetylcholine receptors.
Each end plate potential normally triggers an action potential.
Myasthenia gravis, curare and botulinum toxin disturb the transmission.

abschnitte.titel: From the nerve to the muscle
abschnitte.text: A **motor neuron** is a nerve cell that controls muscles. Its end lies close to a skeletal muscle fibre. This point of contact is called the **motor end plate** or neuromuscular synapse. Here the electrical signal of the nerve is turned into a chemical signal. A motor neuron and all the muscle fibres that it controls together form a **motor unit**. In the eye muscles there are only a few fibres, and in large leg muscles often hundreds to over a thousand.

When an action potential arrives at the nerve ending, voltage-gated **calcium channels** open. The calcium flowing in makes small sacs release their contents, the messenger substance **acetylcholine**. It binds to **nicotinic acetylcholine receptors** in the muscle membrane. These receptors are ion channels that open directly. Mainly **sodium** flows in, a little potassium flows out, and the membrane is depolarised. An enzyme then quickly breaks the acetylcholine down again.

The **end plate potential** that arises in this way is very large. It safely exceeds the threshold and normally triggers an **action potential** in the muscle fibre every time. This is called a high **safety factor**. This is important so that our movements work reliably. Unlike in the brain, nothing is calculated here, and the signal is simply passed on.

In the disease **myasthenia gravis**, the immune system makes antibodies against the acetylcholine receptors. Muscle weakness that gets worse with exertion is typical. The arrow poison **curare** occupies the receptors without opening them, and the muscles are paralysed limp. **Botulinum toxin**, on the other hand, prevents the release of acetylcholine. It splits proteins that the sacs need in order to fuse with the membrane.

gewusst: Curare was used by peoples in South America for hunting with arrows.
Active substances derived from curare are used today in operations to relax muscles.

teile.einleitung: **Mumps** is a contagious viral disease. Typical are fat cheeks, because the salivary glands swell up. Thanks to vaccination, mumps is much rarer today than it used to be.
wichtigste: Mumps is a contagious viral disease.
It is caused by the mumps virus.
The parotid glands swell, and the face looks as if it had hamster cheeks.
You catch it through droplets of saliva.
Often there is also fever and a headache.
In Germany mumps is also called “Ziegenpeter”.
Since the vaccination became available, mumps has been much rarer in Switzerland.

abschnitte.text: In mumps the **parotid glands** swell. They lie in front of and below the ears and make saliva. When they get fat, the face looks like that of a hamster with full cheeks. Often one side swells first and then the other. The swelling is painful, and **chewing** can hurt too. Many children also have a **fever** and a headache and feel weak.

Mumps is caused by the **mumps virus** and passes from person to person. The virus is in the **saliva**. It can be passed on by coughing, sneezing, a kiss on the cheek or drinking from the same glass. Until the first signs appear, usually two to three weeks go by. Some people notice almost nothing of an infection.

There is no special medicine against the virus itself. Anyone who has mumps should **stay at home and rest**. That way you recover better and do not infect anyone. Soft foods are more pleasant, because chewing hurts. For fever and pain the doctor can recommend something. Usually the illness is over after about one to two weeks.

In the past almost every child got mumps, and it was a typical **childhood disease**. Today there is a vaccination, which is usually given together against measles, mumps and rubella. In Switzerland it is recommended for children, in two doses. Since then **far fewer** children get mumps. In Germany the disease is also called **“Ziegenpeter”**, a very old word.

gewusst: Anyone who has had mumps once is usually protected from it for life.
The parotid gland is the largest salivary gland of the human body.

teile.einleitung: **Multiple sclerosis**, MS for short, is a disease of the central nervous system. The body’s own immune system attacks the protective layer around the nerve fibres. The disease runs a different course in every person.
wichtigste: MS is a chronic inflammatory autoimmune disease.
The brain, spinal cord and optic nerves are affected.
The immune system attacks the myelin sheaths of the nerve fibres.
Women are affected about 2 to 3 times as often as men.
The disease usually begins between the ages of 20 and 40.
At the start it usually comes in relapses.
MS lesions can best be shown with an MRI scan.

abschnitte.text: Many nerve fibres are wrapped in a fatty layer, the **myelin sheaths**. They work like insulation and make sure that signals are passed on quickly. In **multiple sclerosis** the body’s own immune system attacks this layer. **Areas of inflammation** appear and later scars, hence the name: sclerosis means hardening, and multiple means many. The **central nervous system** is affected, that is, the brain, spinal cord and optic nerves. The peripheral nerves are usually spared.

MS usually begins in young adulthood, **between the ages of 20 and 40**. It is a common cause of neurological disability in young adults. Like many autoimmune diseases, it affects **women** clearly more often, about 2 to 3 times as often as men. The reasons for this are not yet fully understood. MS is not contagious.

In most people affected, MS at first runs a **relapsing-remitting** course. This means that relapses with new complaints occur, which then go away completely or in part. Later it can turn into a progressive course. A common first sign is an **inflammation of the optic nerve** with blurred vision and pain when moving the eyes. Numbness, tiredness and unsteadiness when walking also occur.

Many people affected notice that their complaints get temporarily worse in **heat**, for example in a hot bath. This is called the **Uhthoff phenomenon**. Heat makes conduction in the damaged nerve fibres worse, and when you cool down it improves again. For the diagnosis, **magnetic resonance imaging** (MRI) is central, because the lesions in the white matter can be seen well in it. MS cannot yet be cured, but medicines can make relapses clearly less frequent.

gewusst: Switzerland is one of the countries where MS is comparatively common.
The name multiple sclerosis describes the many hardened scars in the nervous system.

teile.einleitung: The stomach is a muscular bag in the upper belly where food lands after we have swallowed it. There the food is mixed with gastric juice and broken down further. The stomach is an important station on the long journey of digestion.
wichtigste: After swallowing, food passes through the gullet into the stomach.
In the stomach the food is mixed with gastric juice and broken down.
Gastric juice contains hydrochloric acid, which makes bacteria harmless.
The enzyme pepsin begins the digestion of protein in the stomach.
A layer of mucus protects the stomach wall from its own acid.
In adults the stomach holds about 1.5 litres.
Stomach rumbling often happens when the stomach is empty and contracts.

abschnitte.text: The **stomach** lies in the upper left of the belly, directly below the diaphragm. It has the shape of a curved sack or a bean. At the top the gullet opens into the stomach, and at the bottom it passes into the small intestine. When empty it is quite small, and after a big meal it can stretch a lot.

The stomach wall consists of strong muscles that tighten in waves. This kneads the food pulp, mixes it and breaks it down further. Depending on the meal, food stays in the stomach for about two to four hours, and fatty food for longer. Then the **pylorus**, a ring-shaped muscle at the exit of the stomach, lets the pulp out into the small intestine in portions.

The lining of the stomach makes about two to three litres of **gastric juice** a day. It contains **hydrochloric acid**, which is so strong that it kills most of the bacteria in food. The enzyme pepsin begins to break down protein from meat, cheese or eggs. So that the stomach does not digest itself, a thick layer of mucus protects it.

Even when the stomach is empty, it contracts regularly to push remains along. In doing so, air and liquid are pushed around, which makes gurgling sounds. Because there is no food to muffle the noises, you can hear **stomach rumbling** especially well when the stomach is empty. So it is quite normal and usually a sign of hunger.

Eating too much, too fatty food or too fast can cause tummy ache or heartburn. In **heartburn**, stomach acid rises into the gullet and burns there. In a stomach bug you often have to be sick, and the muscles then press the contents of the stomach upwards. The bacterium Helicobacter pylori can cause stomach ulcers.

Eating slowly and chewing well takes the strain off the stomach, because it has no teeth. Regular meals and enough water are good for it. After eating, a short walk is better than wild romping about. The feeling of being full comes only about 20 minutes after you start eating, so if you wolf your food you can easily eat too much.

begriffe.erklaerung: A tube of muscle that brings food from the mouth to the stomach.
An acid liquid in the stomach that digests food and kills germs.
A ring muscle at the exit of the stomach that lets the food pulp into the intestine.
A protein that breaks food down into smaller building blocks.

gewusst: The lining of the stomach renews itself every few days, so that the acid does not destroy it.
Gastric juice has a pH value of about 1 to 2 and is therefore even more acid than lemon juice.
For discovering that bacteria cause stomach ulcers, Barry Marshall and Robin Warren received the Nobel Prize in 2005.

teile.einleitung: The **middle finger** stands exactly in the middle of the hand. In almost all people it is the longest finger and helps us with writing, playing music and gripping.
wichtigste: The middle finger is the longest finger in most people.
It lies between the index finger and the ring finger.
In piano playing it has the number 3.
When taking an oath in Switzerland you raise the thumb, index finger and middle finger.
From writing, a hard spot often forms on the middle finger.
To snap your fingers you need your thumb and middle finger.

abschnitte.text: Each hand has five fingers: thumb, index finger, middle finger, ring finger and little finger. The **middle finger** stands in the middle. On one side lies the **index finger**, on the other the **ring finger**. In almost all people it is the **longest finger**. Like the index, ring and little fingers, it consists of three finger bones, while the thumb has only two.

In **piano playing** each finger gets a number. You count from the thumb: thumb 1, index finger 2, **middle finger 3**, ring finger 4 and little finger 5. In piano music these numbers are often written above the notes. This way you know which finger to press a key with. This is the same for the left and the right hand.

In Switzerland, when taking an **oath**, you raise three fingers: **thumb, index finger and middle finger**. The ring finger and little finger stay bent. This is how, for example, newly elected members of parliaments swear when they take the oath. The **Rütli Oath** is also often shown with this oath hand. The three fingers are traditionally taken as a sign of the Trinity.

When writing, the pen usually rests on the **middle finger**. The pressure makes a small hard spot, a callus, appear there on many schoolchildren. The middle finger also helps with **snapping**: you press it firmly against the thumb, then it slips off and strikes the heel of the hand. This makes the typical sound.

gewusst: The callus from writing protects the skin, and it gets smaller if you write less by hand.
The sound when snapping arises mainly when the middle finger strikes the heel of the hand.

teile.einleitung: A skeletal muscle consists of many long cells, the **muscle fibres**. They are densely packed with fine protein threads that can slide into one another. This is how the muscle contracts.
wichtigste: A muscle fibre is a single skeletal muscle cell.
It has many cell nuclei.
Muscle fibres are filled with myofibrils.
The smallest working unit of a myofibril is the sarcomere.
Actin and myosin slide past each other during contraction.
ATP supplies the energy for this.
A whole muscle is wrapped in a fascia.

abschnitte.text: In skeletal muscle, a single long muscle cell is called a **muscle fibre**. It can grow to several centimetres long. A muscle fibre arises from many fused precursor cells and therefore has **many cell nuclei**. Several fibres are gathered into bundles, and many bundles form a muscle. A whole muscle is surrounded by a sheath of tough connective tissue, the **fascia**. It holds everything together and lets neighbouring muscles glide past each other.

Each muscle fibre is filled along its length with many thin threads, the **myofibrils**. A myofibril consists of many sections lying one behind the other, the **sarcomeres**. The sarcomere is the smallest working unit of the muscle. In contraction each sarcomere becomes a little shorter. Because thousands lie one behind the other, the whole muscle becomes noticeably shorter.

In the sarcomeres lie two proteins: thin threads of **actin** and thicker ones of **myosin**. The myosin heads grab the actin threads and pull on them. In this way the threads slide into one another, and the muscle shortens. The energy for this is supplied by **ATP** (adenosine triphosphate), the direct energy carrier of the cell. Without ATP, actin and myosin cannot move.

Not all muscle fibres are the same. **Slow red fibres** (type I) have many mitochondria and a lot of red muscle pigment. They tire slowly and are suited to endurance. Fast fibres, on the other hand, quickly supply a lot of force but soon tire. With regular strength training the fibres mainly become **thicker**, which is called hypertrophy.

gewusst: The name sarcomere comes from Greek and means roughly “piece of flesh”.
Under the microscope skeletal muscle fibres look striped, because actin and myosin are arranged regularly.

teile.einleitung: Mast cells are cells of the immune system that sit in the tissue. They are full of small granules containing messenger substances. They play an important part in allergies, for example in the itching after a mosquito bite.
wichtigste: Histamine is stored in the granules of mast cells.
Histamine causes itching and swelling.
Paul Ehrlich described mast cells in the late 19th century.
Their precursors are made in the bone marrow.
The release of the granules is called degranulation.
In mastocytosis, mast cells multiply abnormally.
The enzyme tryptase in the blood shows that mast cells have been activated.

abschnitte.text: The German scientist **Paul Ehrlich** described mast cells in the late **19th century**. Under the microscope they looked plump, because they contain many granules. People therefore took them for especially **well-fed cells**. In German, “mast” means fattening, and from this comes the name **mast cell**. The precursors of mast cells are made in the **bone marrow** and then mature in the tissue.

Mast cells are found mainly where the body comes into contact with the environment. These include the **skin**, the mucous membranes of the airways and the **intestine**. They often lie near small blood vessels. There they can react quickly when foreign substances or germs get in. They help, for example, in fighting parasites and in healing wounds.

In their granules, mast cells store messenger substances, above all **histamine**. When a mast cell is activated, it quickly releases the contents of the granules outwards. This is called **degranulation**. Histamine makes the blood vessels wider and more permeable. This causes **redness**, **swelling** and **itching**. In an **allergy**, mast cells react to substances that are really harmless, such as pollen.

In the rare **mastocytosis**, mast cells multiply abnormally and collect in the tissue. To prove mastocytosis or a strong activation of mast cells, the enzyme **tryptase** is measured in the blood. Against allergic complaints there are **antihistamines**, which block the effect of histamine. A **mast cell stabiliser** such as **cromoglicic acid**, on the other hand, already stops the release of histamine.

gewusst: The weal after a mosquito bite is partly a result of histamine from mast cells.
Paul Ehrlich received the Nobel Prize in Medicine in 1908 together with Ilya Mechnikov.

teile.einleitung: After lunch many people get tired. An **afternoon nap** can then give new strength. Small children need one almost every day, and adults sometimes treat themselves to a short nap.
wichtigste: An afternoon nap is a short sleep after lunch.
A short sleep during the day is also called a nap.
Small children most often need an afternoon nap.
Most children stop having one at about 3 to 5 years old.
For adults about 20 minutes is enough.
An afternoon nap that is too long makes it harder to fall asleep in the evening.
In Spain the midday rest is known as the siesta.

abschnitte.text: **Small children** need a great deal of sleep. The night alone is often not enough for them, so they usually sleep at midday too. Babies even sleep several times a day. In time children need less sleep during the day. Most stop having an afternoon nap between **3 and 5 years old**. Then the sleep at night is enough for them.

For adults a short **nap** of about 10 to 30 minutes is ideal, and often **20 minutes** is given. Such a nap refreshes you and helps you to be alert again. Anyone who sleeps longer falls into deep sleep and often wakes up groggy. In addition you are less tired in the evening, and **falling asleep** is harder. That is why an afternoon nap should not be too long and should not take place too late in the afternoon.

In some countries a midday rest is part of everyday life. Especially well known is the **siesta** in **Spain**. In the hot midday hours many people rest there, and some shops stay closed. The word comes from Latin and refers to the sixth hour of the day, that is, about midday. In other warm countries too, a break at midday is common.

For an afternoon nap, a **quiet, slightly dark room** is suitable. Quiet and little light help you to fall asleep, while noise and bright light keep you awake. A sofa or a comfortable armchair is often enough. In Switzerland many day nurseries have a rest room where the little ones can sleep after eating.

gewusst: The afternoon dip after lunch is also connected with our inner clock, not just with a full belly.
The German word for a nap, “Nickerchen”, comes from the fact that when you fall asleep sitting up, your head often nods forwards.

teile.einleitung: MRSA stands for methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus. This is a form of a common bacterium against which many antibiotics no longer work. Especially in hospitals, MRSA is a well-known problem.
wichtigste: Under the microscope, staphylococci look like balls in grape-shaped clusters.
Many healthy people carry Staphylococcus aureus in the front of the nose.
MRSA was first described in the 1960s.
The resistance to methicillin comes from the gene mecA.
Severe MRSA infections are often treated with vancomycin.
In hospital, consistent hand disinfection is the most important thing.

abschnitte.text: **Staphylococci** are ball-shaped bacteria. Under the microscope they often lie together in **grape-shaped clusters**. This is where the name comes from: the Greek word “staphyle” means grape. The species **Staphylococcus aureus** lives in many healthy people in the **front of the nose** or on the skin without making them ill. But if it gets into wounds or the blood, it can cause infections.

**Antibiotics** are medicines against bacteria. But some bacteria become **resistant**, which means that the medicine no longer works. **Methicillin** is an antibiotic from the penicillin group. Shortly after it was introduced, **MRSA** was first described in the **1960s**. The resistance comes from the gene **mecA**. It makes sure that many antibiotics of this group can no longer attack.

In **hospital** there are many weakened people, often with wounds or catheters. There, MRSA can become dangerous. It is passed on mainly through the **hands**. That is why **consistent hand disinfection** is the most important protective measure. Anyone who carries MRSA is often cared for in a room of their own, and the staff wear protective clothing.

Severe MRSA infections are often treated with the antibiotic **vancomycin**. There are also other drugs. Many people only carry MRSA without being ill. In them a **decolonisation** can be done: the bacteria are removed from the **skin and mucous membranes** with special ointments and washing solutions. To avoid resistance, antibiotics should be taken only when they are really needed.

gewusst: About one in three people carries Staphylococcus aureus in the nose, usually without noticing.
The name “aureus” means “golden”, because the bacteria form golden yellow colonies on culture plates.

teile.einleitung: An mRNA vaccine brings the cells a set of instructions for building a protein of a germ. The cells make this protein briefly, and the immune system gets to know it. Such vaccines became well known during the Covid-19 pandemic.
wichtigste: mRNA is a set of instructions for building a protein.
In the Covid-19 vaccine it is the blueprint for the spike protein.
The mRNA is read at the ribosomes in the cytoplasm.
It does not get into the cell nucleus and does not change the DNA.
Tiny fat envelopes, the lipid nanoparticles, protect the mRNA.
After a few days the cell breaks the mRNA down.

abschnitte.text: **mRNA** stands for messenger RNA. In every cell it carries blueprints from the genetic material to the protein factories. An mRNA vaccine against Covid-19 contains the blueprint for the **spike protein**. This is a protein on the surface of the coronavirus. The cells make this protein for a short time. The **immune system** recognises it as foreign and learns to fight it. If it later meets the real virus, it can react more quickly.

The vaccine mRNA stays in the **cytoplasm**, the inside of the cell outside the nucleus. There the **ribosomes** read it and build the protein. The mRNA does **not get into the cell nucleus** and does not change the DNA. mRNA is a short-lived molecule. After a few days the cell’s own enzymes break it down. What remains is the **immunological memory**.

Free mRNA would quickly break down in the body. That is why it is packed in tiny fat envelopes, the **lipid nanoparticles**. They protect the mRNA and fuse with the cell membrane. In this way the set of instructions gets into the cell. Because mRNA is delicate, the first Covid-19 vaccines had to be stored **deep-frozen**. The vaccine from Pfizer and BioNTech initially needed about **minus 70 degrees Celsius**. This made distribution difficult.

For a long time foreign mRNA caused too strong inflammation in the body. **Katalin Karikó** and **Drew Weissman** discovered that modified building blocks help. In the Covid-19 vaccines the building block **uridine** is replaced by a modified form, N1-methylpseudouridine. In this way the mRNA is recognised less as foreign, and more protein is made. For this work the two received the **Nobel Prize** in Physiology or Medicine in **2023**.

In Switzerland the authority **Swissmedic** checks whether a vaccine is safe and effective. In **December 2020** it approved the mRNA vaccine from Pfizer and BioNTech. It was the first Covid-19 vaccine approved in Switzerland.

gewusst: The idea of using mRNA as a medicine was being researched decades before the Covid-19 pandemic.
An mRNA vaccine does not contain a whole virus, only the blueprint for a single protein.

teile.einleitung: In almost every cell of our body, tiny **mitochondria** are at work. They are often called the “powerhouse of the cell”, because they obtain energy from nutrients.
wichtigste: Mitochondria are cell organelles and are regarded as the power stations of the cell.
Cell respiration takes place in them.
For this they need oxygen.
They make the energy carrier ATP.
A mitochondrion has two membranes, and the inner one is strongly folded.
The folds are called cristae.
According to the endosymbiont theory, mitochondria were once independent bacteria.

abschnitte.text: A **mitochondrion** is a **cell organelle**, that is, a small component with a particular job in the cell. Here energy is obtained from nutrients, hence the comparison with a power station. The energy is stored in the molecule **ATP** (adenosine triphosphate). ATP is the energy currency of the cell. Muscles need it, for example, to contract, and the brain needs it for thinking.

In the mitochondria, **cell respiration** takes place. In it, sugar is broken down step by step and energy is released. This needs **oxygen**. We breathe it in with the lungs, and the blood carries it to every cell. Without oxygen, mitochondria cannot break down sugar completely. Carbon dioxide and water are produced as waste, and we breathe the carbon dioxide out again.

A mitochondrion has **two membranes**, a smooth outer one and an inner one. The inner membrane is strongly folded. These folds are called **cristae**, which is Latin and means crests. The folds create a large surface. There sit the proteins that supply most of the energy for the cell.

Cells that need a lot of energy have especially many mitochondria. A good example is the **heart muscle cells**. The heart works without a break, day and night. A large part of its cell volume therefore consists of mitochondria. Muscle and nerve cells are also well equipped with them. Red blood cells, on the other hand, have none at all.

abschnitte.titel: Once living things of their own
abschnitte.text: The **endosymbiont theory** explains where mitochondria come from. A very long time ago, bacteria were taken in by larger cells. They were not digested but went on living inside and worked together with the cell. In time they became organelles. One clue to this is that mitochondria still have **their own DNA** today.

gewusst: Mitochondria have their own genetic material, separate from the genetic material in the cell nucleus.
Red blood cells have no mitochondria, so that they do not use up the oxygen themselves.

teile.einleitung: **Mineralocorticoids** are hormones from the adrenal cortex. They regulate how much salt and water the body keeps. The most important of them is **aldosterone**.
wichtigste: The most important mineralocorticoid in humans is aldosterone.
It is made in the adrenal cortex.
In the kidney, aldosterone takes sodium back and lets potassium be passed out.
With the sodium, the body also holds back water.
The enzyme renin from the kidney sets off the chain leading to the release of aldosterone.
ANP from the atria of the heart acts as its opponent.

abschnitte.text: The name says it: mineralocorticoids regulate the **minerals**, above all **sodium** and **potassium**. They are made in the outermost layer of the **adrenal cortex**. The most important is **aldosterone**. In the kidney it acts in the distal tubule and the collecting duct. There it makes sure that sodium is taken back into the blood and, in exchange, potassium is passed out in the urine. Because water follows sodium, more water stays in the body and blood pressure rises.

If the blood pressure in the kidney falls, it releases the enzyme **renin**. Renin starts a chain of steps that ends with **angiotensin II**. This substance narrows blood vessels and stimulates the adrenal cortex to release aldosterone. Experts call the whole thing the **renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system**. It helps the body to keep blood pressure and blood volume steady.

If there is a lot of blood in the circulation, the **atria of the heart** are stretched. They then release the hormone **ANP**, the atrial natriuretic peptide. ANP inhibits the release of aldosterone. The kidney then passes out more sodium and water. In this way the heart itself puts on the brakes when there is too much fluid in the body.

In **Conn’s syndrome**, the adrenal cortex makes too much aldosterone. High blood pressure and a low potassium level are typical. In **Addison’s disease**, the adrenal cortex is usually destroyed by the body’s own immune system, and cortisol and aldosterone are missing. Then low blood pressure and a craving for salt can occur. As a replacement for aldosterone, **fludrocortisone** is given. The medicine **spironolactone**, on the other hand, blocks the aldosterone receptor and acts as a potassium-sparing diuretic.

gewusst: Without aldosterone the body would lose so much salt that blood pressure could fall dangerously.
Spironolactone is called potassium-sparing because sodium and water are passed out but potassium stays in the body.

teile.einleitung: Marcel Hug is one of the most successful wheelchair athletes in the world. The Swiss has been winning big races on the track and on the road for many years. His nickname is “Silver Bullet”.
