wichtigste: Marcel Hug is a Swiss wheelchair track and road athlete.
He comes from the canton of Thurgau.
His nickname is “Silver Bullet”.
He has won several gold medals at the Paralympic Games.
He has won many big marathons, for example in Boston, London and Berlin.

abschnitte.text: **Marcel Hug** was born in 1986 and grew up in the **canton of Thurgau**. He has used a **wheelchair** since birth and began wheelchair sport as a child. He races over short and long distances, from the track to the **marathon**. At the **Paralympic Games** he has won several gold medals, for example in Rio de Janeiro in 2016 and in Tokyo in 2021.

He got his nickname **“Silver Bullet”** because of his **silver helmet**. The name also fits because he is very fast in his racing wheelchair. At big marathons such as those in **Boston**, **London**, **Berlin** or **New York** he has often stood at the top of the podium.

A **racing wheelchair** looks quite different from an everyday wheelchair. It has three wheels and is built long and low. It is driven with the arms, using push rims on the wheels. For this you need a great deal of **strength** and **stamina** in the arms, shoulders and trunk. In **Nottwil** in the canton of Lucerne stands the Swiss Paraplegic Centre, where many wheelchair athletes train.

gewusst: Marcel Hug has been named Swiss Disabled Sportsperson of the Year several times.

teile.einleitung: Muscles are the motors of our body. Without them we could neither move an arm nor run, breathe or smile. A muscle works by contracting and pulling on bones as it does so.
wichtigste: Muscles move the body by contracting.
There are skeletal, heart and smooth muscles.
A tendon joins a muscle to a bone.
Muscles can only pull, not push, so every skeletal muscle needs an opposing muscle.
The biceps bends the arm, and the triceps straightens it.
On the inside a skeletal muscle consists of bundles of muscle fibres.
Regular exercise makes muscles stronger.
Muscle pain the day after a lot of sport is called sore muscles.

abschnitte.text: A **muscle** is a tissue that can contract. Humans have over 600 skeletal muscles, which together can make up almost half of body weight. When a muscle works, it becomes shorter and thicker. In doing so it uses energy from food and produces heat, which is why we get warm when doing sport.

A skeletal muscle is built from many **muscle fibres** that are gathered into bundles, rather like threads in a rope. Each fibre is a long cell that can be up to several centimetres long. Inside lie tiny protein threads that slide into one another when the muscle contracts. At both ends the muscle turns into a **tendon**, which fixes it to the bone.

The **skeletal muscles** move arms, legs and the whole body, and they obey our will. The **smooth muscles** are found in the stomach, intestine, bladder and blood vessels and work by themselves. The **heart muscle** pumps blood for a whole life without ever getting tired. Only the skeletal muscles can we control consciously.

Muscles can only pull, not push. That is why they work in pairs: the **biceps** at the front of the upper arm bends the arm, and the **triceps** at the back straightens it again. While one contracts, the other relaxes. The muscles at the front and back of the thigh work in a similar way, for example.

Through regular exercise muscle fibres become thicker and stronger, and the muscle becomes more enduring. Anyone who does not move, on the other hand, loses muscle strength, for example after weeks in a plaster cast. After unaccustomed effort tiny tears appear in the fibres, which hurt the next day. That is **sore muscles**. They heal by themselves after a few days.

Muscles need **protein** from foods such as dairy products, eggs, fish, meat or pulses. Warming up before sport protects against strains. Enough sleep is important, because muscles recover and grow during rest. Stretching also keeps the muscles supple.

begriffe.erklaerung: A firm band that joins a muscle to a bone.
A long muscle cell that can contract.
A muscle that carries out the opposite movement.
Muscle pain after unaccustomed effort.

gewusst: The largest muscle of the human body is the gluteus maximus, and one of the smallest sits in the ear on the stirrup bone.
For a smile you need only a few muscles in the face, and altogether there are over 40 muscles in the face.
The heart is a muscle that beats about three billion times in a lifetime.

teile.einleitung: In the knee joint lie two crescent-shaped discs of cartilage, the menisci. They cushion shocks and make sure the knee is stable. In sports with a lot of twisting they can be injured.
wichtigste: A meniscus consists of fibrous cartilage.
The Greek word means “little moon”.
The menisci lie between the thigh bone and the shin bone.
They cushion and spread the pressure over a larger area.
The inner meniscus tears much more often than the outer one.
A tear often happens when twisting on a bent knee that is bearing weight.
Surgery is mostly done with keyhole surgery of the joint.

abschnitte.text: The name **meniscus** comes from Greek and means **“little moon”**. The menisci have the shape of a crescent moon. In each knee there are two: the **inner meniscus** and the **outer meniscus**. They lie between the **thigh bone** and the **shin bone**. They consist of **fibrous cartilage**, a firm but still slightly elastic tissue.

The joint surfaces of the thigh and shin do not fit together exactly. The menisci make up for this. They **cushion shocks**, for example when jumping and running. They also **enlarge the contact surface** and **spread the pressure** more evenly. This protects the cartilage of the joint. In addition the menisci make the knee more stable.

A meniscus tears especially easily when **twisting on a bent knee that is bearing weight**. This happens in football, skiing or tennis, for example. The **inner meniscus** tears **much more often**, because it is more firmly joined to the inner ligament and is therefore less mobile. In older people a meniscus can also tear through wear, sometimes with just a simple movement.

After a tear the knee often hurts when bending or twisting, and it can swell. If a torn piece gets caught in the joint, the knee suddenly **cannot be straightened completely**. This is then called a locked joint. To investigate, an **MRI** is often done, in which the menisci can be seen well.

Not every tear has to be operated on. When surgery is done, today it is mostly with **keyhole surgery of the joint**, **arthroscopy**. In this, a camera and fine instruments are put into the knee through small cuts. A tear in the outer edge can often be stitched. In the **inner part**, however, a tear **heals badly**, because this part has **hardly any blood supply**. There, often only the damaged piece is removed.

gewusst: The jaw joint also has a disc of cartilage that works rather like a meniscus.
Doctors today try to keep as much of the meniscus as possible, because it protects the knee in the long term.

teile.einleitung: Dairy products are made from milk. They include cheese, yoghurt, quark, butter and cream. In Switzerland they have a long tradition, and many specialities are world-famous.
wichtigste: Quark, yoghurt, cheese, butter and cream are dairy products.
In Switzerland most milk comes from cows.
In Switzerland the German word for cream is “Rahm” rather than “Sahne”.
If cream is whipped for a very long time, butter is made.
In cheese-making, yellowish whey is left over.
Emmental is known for its big holes.
Opened milk belongs in the fridge.

abschnitte.text: In Switzerland most milk comes from **cows**. There is also milk from goats and sheep. Many farms keep dairy cows, and in summer many animals graze in the **Alps**. Milk contains protein, fat, milk sugar and **calcium**, which is important for the bones. Many different **dairy products** are made from it.

Dairy products include **yoghurt**, **quark**, **cheese**, **butter** and **cream**. In Switzerland people say **Rahm** for cream, and in Germany rather Sahne. To make yoghurt, certain bacteria are added to the milk, which make it thick and slightly sour. If you whip cream, it first becomes whipped cream. If you keep whipping for **a very long time**, the fat separates off, and **butter** is made.

In **cheese-making**, the milk is curdled with rennet or bacteria. Then the mass is cut up. In this, the solid cheese mass separates from a yellowish liquid, the **whey**. The cheese mass is pressed into moulds, salted and then often matures for months in a cellar. Whey is used, for example, as a drink or animal feed.

Switzerland is known for its cheese. **Emmental** has **big holes**. They arise from gases that bacteria make during ripening. Other well-known kinds are Gruyère, Appenzeller and Sbrinz. A popular dish is **fondue**: melted cheese is put on the table in a shared pot, the caquelon. You dip pieces of bread into it with long forks.

Dairy products are delicate and go off quickly when it is warm. **Opened milk** therefore belongs in the **fridge** and should be drunk soon. Yoghurt, quark and cream are also kept cool. Hard cheese keeps longer because it contains little water. The packaging shows how long a product will keep at least.

gewusst: For one kilogram of Emmental you need about 12 litres of milk.
In Switzerland there are several hundred different kinds of cheese.

teile.einleitung: Muscles consist of different **muscle fibre types**. Some fibres are slow and enduring, others fast and strong but quick to tire. The mixture helps to decide whether someone is more likely to run a marathon or to sprint.
wichtigste: Type I fibres are slow and enduring.
Type IIx fibres contract fastest and tire most quickly.
Type IIa fibres lie in between and work oxidatively and glycolytically.
Myoglobin gives type I fibres their red colour.
Marathon runners usually have many type I fibres in their legs.
Classically the types are told apart by the activity of myosin ATPase.

abschnitte.text: **Type I fibres** contract slowly but hardly tire. They are also called **slow-twitch fibres**. They get their energy **oxidatively**, that is, with oxygen. That is why they have many mitochondria and are surrounded by especially many **capillaries**, which make short routes for the oxygen. Their red colour comes from **myoglobin**, a pigment that stores oxygen in the muscle.

**Type IIa fibres** are fast and **oxidative and glycolytic**. They can get energy both with and without oxygen and so lie between type I and type IIx. **Type IIx fibres** contract fastest. They get their energy mainly **glycolytically**, that is, from the quick breakdown of sugar without oxygen. In return they tire after a short time. Because they contain little myoglobin, they look paler.

Classically the fibre types are told apart **histochemically**, that is, by staining tissue samples. What matters is the activity of **myosin ATPase**. Different forms of myosin split ATP at different speeds. This speed also decides how quickly the fibre contracts.

**Marathon runners** often have clearly more than half type I fibres in their leg muscles. **Sprinters**, on the other hand, have many fast type II fibres. In a movement the fibres are used according to the **size principle**, which is also called Henneman’s principle. First small motor units with slow fibres work. Only when a lot of force is needed do the large, fast units join in.

gewusst: The dark meat of a chicken leg contains more enduring red fibres than the pale breast.
How many fast and slow fibres someone has depends strongly on their inherited traits.

teile.einleitung: Tiredness is a sign from the body: it needs a break and sleep. Someone who is tired finds it harder to concentrate and reacts more slowly.
wichtigste: Tiredness shows that the body and brain need rest.
Heavy eyes and frequent yawning are typical.
Only real sleep helps against tiredness.
The hormone melatonin makes us tired in the evening.
Too little sleep makes you unable to concentrate and in a bad mood.
Caffeine, for example in cola, can disturb falling asleep.
Anyone who rides a bike when tired reacts more slowly.

abschnitte.text: When the body needs sleep, the **eyelids become heavy** and almost close by themselves. You yawn often, rub your eyes and have less strength. Many people also become **irritable** and in a bad mood. Anyone who wakes up fit in the morning and stays lively during the day has usually had enough sleep.

In the evening, when it gets dark, the body makes the hormone **melatonin**. It tells the body that it is now time for sleep. Bright light, especially from screens, can slow the production of melatonin. That is why it is good to put your phone and tablet away before sleeping. A dark, quiet room helps you to fall asleep.

A tired **brain** works more slowly. You find it harder to pay attention and remember less. In sleep the brain sorts out what you have learned during the day. Children of school age therefore need a lot of sleep, usually about 9 to 11 hours a night. Regular bedtimes help the body to get into a good rhythm.

Someone who is very tired **reacts more slowly** and overlooks dangers more easily. In road traffic, for example on a bike, this can lead to accidents. Adults too should not drive tired. When you are very tired, only a break or sleep helps, not a trick.

Drinks such as coffee, cola or energy drinks contain **caffeine**. Caffeine keeps you awake for a while but does not replace sleep. It can disturb falling asleep and is not suitable for children. Much better against tiredness are enough sleep, exercise in the fresh air and drinking enough water.

gewusst: Yawning is catching: if you see someone yawn, you often have to yawn yourself.
While you sleep, not only the muscles but also the brain recover.

teile.einleitung: The lymphatic system is a fine network of vessels and organs that runs through the whole body. It carries tissue fluid back into the blood and supports the body’s defence. The lymph nodes that you can sometimes feel in your neck during a cold belong to it.
wichtigste: The lymphatic system carries tissue fluid and supports the immune defence.
The liquid in the lymph vessels is called lymph.
Lymph nodes filter the lymph and hold germs back.
The spleen, thymus and tonsils also belong to the lymphatic system.
Many lymphocytes, a kind of white blood cell, live in the lymph.
The lymphatic system has no heart of its own, and the lymph is pushed along by muscle movements.
Swollen lymph nodes often show that the body is fighting an infection.

abschnitte.text: A little liquid constantly seeps out of the fine blood vessels into the tissue to supply the cells. Most of it flows back into the blood, but some stays between the cells. The **lymph vessels** collect this tissue fluid, and then it is called **lymph**. It is pale and slightly yellowish and contains many defence cells.

Lymph vessels begin very fine in the tissue and join up into ever larger vessels. The largest is the thoracic duct, which leads the lymph into a large vein near the neck. In this way the liquid returns to the blood. Valves in the vessels make sure that the lymph flows in one direction only.

On its way the lymph flows through **lymph nodes**, small bean-shaped filter stations. Humans have several hundred of them, especially many in the neck, the armpits, the groin and the belly. In the lymph nodes, **lymphocytes** wait for germs and fight them. In an infection the lymph nodes swell, because the defence cells multiply strongly there.

Besides the lymph nodes, other organs belong to the lymphatic system. The **spleen** in the upper left of the belly filters the blood. In the **thymus** behind the breastbone, the T lymphocytes mature in children. The tonsils in the throat catch germs that get in through the mouth and nose.

In the intestine the lymphatic system has a special job. Fat from food is not taken up straight into the blood, but first into the lymph vessels of the intestinal villi. After a fatty meal the lymph there therefore looks milky white. This is also where the German name for the thoracic duct, “milk-chest duct”, comes from.

The lymphatic system has no pump of its own like the heart. The lymph is pushed along by the movement of the muscles and by breathing. That is why your feet can swell after sitting or standing for a long time. If the lymph backs up for good, a **lymphoedema** develops, which is treated with a special massage, lymphatic drainage.

begriffe.erklaerung: A pale liquid that flows in the lymph vessels.
A small filter station in which defence cells fight germs.
A white blood cell that fights germs in a targeted way.
A swelling caused by too much liquid in the tissue.

gewusst: About two to three litres of lymph flow back into the blood every day.
In a sore throat the doctor often feels the lymph nodes in the neck, because they are then swollen.
Movement is important for the flow of lymph, because the muscles push the lymph along like a pump.

teile.einleitung: A height chart hangs on the wall in many children’s rooms or kitchens. You can read off how tall you are. With marks and dates you can even see how quickly you are growing.
wichtigste: With a height chart you measure body height.
You stand in front of it barefoot and straight.
A book or a board laid flat on the head shows the exact height.
The zero of the height chart must be at the floor.
100 centimetres are 1 metre.
A centimetre has 10 millimetres.

abschnitte.text: A **height chart** is a long strip of wood, paper or plastic with a **centimetre scale**. You fix it upright on the wall. For it to measure correctly, the **zero must be exactly at the floor**. If it hangs too high or too low, none of the numbers are right. So when you hang it, it is best to check with a metre rule.

For an exact measurement you stand **barefoot** and **straight** with your back to the wall. Heels, bottom and the back of the head touch the wall, and you look straight ahead. A second person lays a **book** or a **board** flat on the head so that it touches the wall. Where the book touches the height chart, they make a mark. This way hair or a crooked look does not show a wrong value.

On the height chart there are mostly **centimetres**. **100 centimetres** are exactly **1 metre**. If a mark is at 100 cm, the child is 1 metre tall. Between two centimetres you often see even smaller marks. These are **millimetres**, and **1 centimetre has 10 millimetres**. This way you can read it off very precisely.

Next to each mark you often write the **date** and the name. This way you can see later **when you were that tall**. An example: Leo’s mark last year was at **110 cm**, and today it is at **117 cm**. So Leo has grown **7 cm**. Children do not always grow at the same speed, and sometimes there are real growth spurts.

gewusst: In the morning you are slightly taller than in the evening, because the discs in the back are pressed together a little during the day.
Doctors enter children’s heights on growth charts to follow their development.

teile.einleitung: After a tiring day of sport the muscles sometimes hurt, often only the next morning. That is **sore muscles**. They are unpleasant but harmless and go away by themselves.
wichtigste: You usually feel sore muscles on the next day or the day after.
They arise from tiny tears in the muscle fibres.
Mainly unaccustomed or very tiring movements set them off.
They usually last a few days.
Rest and light movement help.
Sore muscles are not dangerous.
If you repeat an exercise regularly, they get weaker.

abschnitte.text: If a muscle has to do something **unaccustomed** or very tiring, **tiny tears** appear in the muscle fibres. The body repairs these small injuries, and the tissue swells slightly as it does so. This hurts for a while. Sore muscles arise exactly in the muscles that have worked. After lots of sit-ups you therefore feel them in the **stomach**, and after a long bike ride more in the legs.

Sore muscles usually begin only **hours after the sport**. You often feel them most strongly on the next day or the day after. After **a few days** they are usually gone again, at the latest after about a week. Sore muscles are **not dangerous**, and the muscle heals by itself. Strong pain right during the sport, on the other hand, is more likely a sign of an injury.

You get sore muscles especially easily when the muscle has to **brake**. A good example is a hike **steeply downhill**. With every step the thighs have to catch the body. This braking work puts the fibres under heavy strain. Anyone who walks a long descent in the Swiss mountains often notices this clearly the next day.

Above all the muscle needs **time** to heal. **Rest** and relaxed movement, such as a walk, do many people good. A **warm bath** can also be pleasant. You should only do hard exercise again when the pain has gone. Anyone who repeats a new exercise every week usually gets **less and less** sore muscle, because the muscle gets used to it.

gewusst: It used to be believed that lactic acid in the muscle was to blame for sore muscles, but this is now considered disproved.
Even a single training session protects the muscle for some time from getting severe sore muscles again with the same exercise.

teile.einleitung: Lymph nodes are small organs spread all over the body. They filter the lymph and help the body to fight off germs. In a cold you can sometimes feel them in your neck.
wichtigste: Lymph nodes belong to the lymphatic system.
The lymph is filtered in them.
The lymph vessels carry the lymph to the lymph nodes.
An adult has about 600 lymph nodes.
Lymph nodes are bean-shaped and contain many lymphocytes.
In an infection they swell, because defence cells multiply strongly there.

abschnitte.text: **Lymph nodes** are small, **bean-shaped** organs. Most are only a few millimetres to about a centimetre across. An adult has about **600** of them. Many lie in the **neck**, in the armpits, in the groin and in the belly. They belong to the **lymphatic system**, a network of vessels and organs that helps with defence.

Besides blood, **lymph**, a pale liquid, also flows through the body. It is collected by the **lymph vessels** and carried to the lymph nodes. There it is **filtered**. Germs, dead cells and foreign substances get caught. Then the lymph flows on and finally reaches the blood.

In the lymph nodes there are particularly many **lymphocytes**. These are defence cells, a kind of white blood cell. When they meet germs, they recognise them and **multiply strongly**. That is why lymph nodes often **swell** in an infection and can be sore to the touch. In a cold you can often feel them well in the **neck**.

Swollen lymph nodes in a cold or sore throat are usually harmless. They get smaller again when the illness is over. But if they stay big for a long time without your being ill, or if they are very hard, you should have this checked by a doctor. That is why doctors often feel the lymph nodes during an examination.

gewusst: The tonsils in the throat also belong to the lymphatic system.
The spleen is the largest organ of the lymphatic system.

teile.einleitung: For us to move, for the heart to beat and for food to travel through the intestine, we need **muscle tissue**. There are three kinds: skeletal muscle, heart muscle and smooth muscle.
wichtigste: There are skeletal muscle, heart muscle and smooth muscle.
Heart muscle is striated but works involuntarily.
In contraction actin and myosin slide past each other.
Calcium ions from the sarcoplasmic reticulum trigger the contraction.
ATP releases the myosin heads from the actin again.
The messenger substance at the motor end plate is acetylcholine.

abschnitte.text: The **skeletal muscle** moves the bones and can be controlled at will. Under the microscope it shows cross striping. The **heart muscle** is also **striated**, but works **involuntarily**. It is steered by a system of its own that produces the excitation. The **smooth muscle** is found, for example, in the intestine, blood vessels and bladder. It has no cross striping and also works by itself.

In contraction the protein threads **actin** and **myosin** slide past each other. The myosin heads pull on the actin filaments and push them towards each other. In this way the muscle shortens without the filaments themselves becoming shorter. The trigger is **calcium ions** from the **sarcoplasmic reticulum**, a store in the muscle cell. Calcium binds to troponin and frees the binding sites on the actin. For the heads to let go again, **ATP** is needed.

Every voluntary movement begins with a signal from a nerve. The point of contact between a motor nerve fibre and a skeletal muscle fibre is called the **motor end plate**. There the messenger substance **acetylcholine** is released. It binds to receptors in the muscle membrane and opens ion channels. The arrow poison **curare** blocks these receptors and in this way paralyses the muscles.

**Skeletal muscle fibres** have many cell nuclei. They arise during development when many single-nucleus precursor cells, the **myoblasts**, fuse with each other. Such a structure is called a **syncytium**. Heart muscle cells, on the other hand, are joined by **intercalated discs**. These contain adhesive junctions and gap junctions, small channels through which the excitation spreads quickly from cell to cell.

gewusst: After death ATP is missing, so actin and myosin no longer let go and the muscles become firm in rigor mortis.
Thanks to its own pacemaker, the heart keeps beating even if the nerves to the heart are cut.

teile.einleitung: **Minerals** are vital substances that the body cannot make itself. We take them in with food and drink. They build bones and teeth and help nerves and muscles to work.
wichtigste: Minerals have to be taken in with food.
The body needs bulk elements such as calcium in larger amounts, and trace elements only in tiny traces.
Calcium is the main building block of bones and teeth.
Vitamin D helps the gut to take up calcium.
Table salt is sodium chloride, and the WHO recommends less than 5 g a day.
Magnesium is important for muscles and nerves.
When you sweat, you lose mainly sodium.

abschnitte.text: Minerals are divided into two groups. **Bulk elements** such as calcium, magnesium, sodium, potassium and chloride occur in the body in larger amounts. **Trace elements** such as iron, iodine, zinc or fluoride are needed only in tiny traces. Both groups are important. Because the body cannot make minerals itself, we have to take them in with **food**. A varied diet usually supplies enough of them.

**Calcium** makes bones and teeth hard and firm. Good sources are milk and dairy products such as cheese and yoghurt, but also some mineral waters and green vegetables. So that the gut can take up calcium well, it needs **vitamin D**. Our skin makes this vitamin with the help of sunlight. Calcium also helps with muscle work and blood clotting.

Table salt consists chemically of **sodium** and **chloride**, and its formula is NaCl. Sodium regulates the water balance and helps to pass on nerve signals. The **World Health Organization** recommends adults less than **5 g of salt** a day, about one teaspoon. In Switzerland people eat clearly more on average, often hidden in bread, cheese or ready meals. When you sweat, the body loses sodium, which is why sweat tastes salty.

**Magnesium** plays a part in muscle relaxation and the conduction of nerves. Many people take it for cramps in the calves. It is found in nuts, wholegrain and green vegetables. Green leafy vegetables such as spinach contain a lot of it, because every **chlorophyll** molecule carries a magnesium atom in its centre. The trace element **iron** is important for the red blood pigment that carries oxygen.

gewusst: As early as 1922 Switzerland introduced iodised table salt, to fight goitre, which was common at the time.
Without the magnesium in chlorophyll, plant leaves would not be green.

teile.einleitung: The spleen is a soft organ the size of a fist in the upper left of the belly. It filters old blood cells out of the blood and supports the immune system in fighting germs. Although it is important, in an emergency you can also live without a spleen.
wichtigste: The spleen lies in the upper left of the belly behind the lower ribs.
It filters old and damaged red blood cells out of the blood.
The spleen supports the immune system and belongs to the lymphatic system.
Many white blood cells live in it that fight germs in the blood.
A healthy spleen is about as big as a fist and weighs around 150 grams.
In a serious accident the spleen can rupture and bleed heavily.
You can live without a spleen but are more prone to certain infections.

abschnitte.text: The **spleen** lies at the top left of the belly, between the stomach and the diaphragm, protected by the lower ribs. It is dark red, soft and about 11 centimetres long. In adults it weighs about 150 grams. Because it has a very good blood supply, a lot of blood constantly flows through it.

Red blood cells live for about 120 days, and then they become old and stiff. In the spleen they have to squeeze through very narrow gaps. Old, stiff cells get stuck and are broken down by **eating cells**. The iron from them is reused to make new red blood cells.

The spleen is the largest organ of the **lymphatic system**. In its inside, the white pulp, sit many **lymphocytes**. They recognise bacteria and other germs in the blood and make antibodies against them. In this way the spleen catches invaders that have got straight into the blood.

In an unborn child the spleen itself makes **blood cells** for a time. After birth the bone marrow takes over this job. Later, however, the spleen still stores platelets and a small reserve of blood cells. In some animals such as the horse, it can release a lot of stored blood during exertion.

abschnitte.titel: A ruptured spleen and life without a spleen
abschnitte.text: In a heavy blow to the belly, for example in a cycling or skiing accident, the spleen can rupture. A **ruptured spleen** is dangerous because it bleeds heavily into the belly. Sometimes the spleen then has to be removed by surgery. Without a spleen the liver and lymph nodes take over some of its jobs, but people affected should make sure they are vaccinated especially well.

Many people know the **stitch** when running, often on the left or right side. In the past people believed that it came from the spleen tightening during sport. Today we know that the exact cause has still not been clearly established. It probably has to do with the diaphragm and the ligaments in the belly.

begriffe.erklaerung: An organ in the upper left of the belly that filters blood and helps with defence.
The soft inner tissue of the spleen.
A defence cell that swallows old cells and germs.
A network of vessels and organs that carries tissue fluid and defends the body.

gewusst: The spleen filters about one twentieth of all the blood every minute.
Some people have one or more small extra spleens besides the spleen.
In glandular fever the spleen can swell greatly, so people who are ill should not do contact sport for a while.

teile.einleitung: Magnetic resonance imaging, or MRI for short, is a method with which doctors can look inside the body without opening it. It produces very detailed cross-section images. For this it needs a strong magnetic field and radio waves.
wichtigste: MRI produces images using a strong magnetic field and radio waves.
It is also called nuclear magnetic resonance imaging.
It does not use X-rays.
Soft tissues such as the brain, ligaments and cartilage can be seen especially well.
The strength of the magnetic field is measured in tesla.
Metal objects have to be taken off beforehand.
During the examination you hear loud knocking noises.

abschnitte.text: Our body consists largely of **water**. Water contains **hydrogen atoms**. Their nuclei behave like tiny magnets. In the strong **magnetic field** of the machine they line up. Then the machine sends **radio waves** into the body. The atomic nuclei then send weak signals back, and a computer works out cross-section images from them.

abschnitte.titel: What you can see with it
abschnitte.text: MRI is especially suitable for **soft tissues**. With it you can show the **brain**, the spinal cord, muscles, **ligaments** and **cartilage** very precisely. That is why it is often used after sports injuries to the knee or for headaches. A big advantage over computed tomography (CT) is that MRI uses **no X-rays**.

You lie on a couch that slides into a narrow tube. During the scans you have to lie as still as possible. The machine makes loud **knocking and humming noises**, so you are often given headphones or earplugs. Beforehand, all **metal objects** have to be taken off, such as jewellery, hair slides or keys. This is because the strong magnetic field pulls metal very powerfully.

The strength of a magnetic field is measured in **tesla**. Many machines in hospitals work with 1.5 or 3 tesla. That is much stronger than a fridge magnet. So that the magnet can be so strong, in many machines it is cooled to a very low temperature with liquid helium. The unit tesla is named after the inventor **Nikola Tesla**.

The chemist **Richard Ernst** of **ETH Zurich** received the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in **1991**. He had developed methods of **nuclear magnetic resonance** that are also important for MRI. That is why the process is also called **nuclear magnetic resonance imaging**. In 2003 Paul Lauterbur and Peter Mansfield received the Nobel Prize in Medicine for their work on imaging with MRI.

gewusst: An MRI magnet is switched on even when nobody is being examined.
With MRI you can even see which areas of the brain are especially active at that moment.

teile.einleitung: Our body grows and heals because cells divide. In **mitosis** the cell nucleus divides so that two daughter cells with exactly the same genetic material arise.
wichtigste: Mitosis is the division of the cell nucleus.
Its phases are called prophase, metaphase, anaphase and telophase.
In anaphase the sister chromatids are pulled to the poles of the cell.
The spindle fibres attach to the kinetochore.
The sister chromatids are joined together at the centromere.
After the division of the nucleus comes cytokinesis, the division of the cytoplasm.

abschnitte.text: Before a cell divides, it doubles its genetic material. After this, each chromosome consists of two identical halves, the **sister chromatids**. They are joined together at a narrowed spot, the **centromere**. A ring-shaped protein complex called **cohesin** holds them tightly enclosed. Mitosis itself runs in four classic phases: **prophase, metaphase, anaphase and telophase**.

In **prophase** the chromatin condenses strongly. The chromosomes thereby become visible as threads in the **light microscope**. At the same time the **spindle apparatus** forms from fine tubes, the microtubules. The spindle fibres bind to the **kinetochore**, a protein complex at the centromere. In **metaphase** all the chromosomes line up in the middle of the cell in one plane.

At the start of **anaphase**, the enzyme **separase** splits the cohesin. Only now can the sister chromatids come apart from each other. The spindle fibres pull them to the opposite **poles of the cell**. In this way each side gets a complete set of chromosomes. This step has to run very precisely, so that no daughter cell receives too many or too few chromosomes.

In **telophase** the chromosomes uncoil again. Around the two sets of chromosomes, new **nuclear envelopes** form, and the nucleoli also form anew. This completes the division of the nucleus, karyokinesis. After this comes **cytokinesis**, the division of the cytoplasm. In animal cells a **contractile ring** of actin and myosin under the membrane tightens and pinches the cell in two daughter cells.

gewusst: The name mitosis comes from the German scientist Walther Flemming, who observed the division of the nucleus closely in the 19th century.
In our body countless cells divide every day, for example in the skin and in the gut.

teile.einleitung: The body needs micronutrients only in small amounts, but they are vital. They include vitamins and minerals. If they are missing, you can fall ill even if you eat enough.
wichtigste: Micronutrients include vitamins and minerals.
According to the WHO, iron deficiency is the most common deficiency in the world.
Iron is needed in haemoglobin for carrying oxygen.
The body needs vitamin K for blood clotting.
On a vegan diet you have to supplement vitamin B12.
A severe lack of vitamin B1 leads to beriberi.
Calcium is the most common mineral in the body.

abschnitte.text: Food gives us **macronutrients** such as carbohydrates, fats and proteins. They give energy. **Micronutrients**, on the other hand, are needed by the body only in tiny amounts. These include **vitamins** and **minerals**. Minerals of which we need only traces are called **trace elements**, for example iron, zinc or iodine. Micronutrients provide no energy but are needed for many processes in the body.

**Iron** is found in the red blood pigment **haemoglobin**. It is needed so that the blood can **carry oxygen**. According to the **WHO**, **iron deficiency** is the most common deficiency of a micronutrient in the world. It makes you tired and pale. **Calcium** is the mineral that occurs in the largest amount in the body. Most of it is in the **bones** and teeth. Dairy products are a good source.

The body needs **vitamin K** for **blood clotting**, so that wounds stop bleeding. It is found mainly in green vegetables. **Vitamin B12** occurs almost only in foods from animals. Anyone on a **vegan** diet therefore usually has to take it as a **supplement**. **Folic acid** is another B vitamin that is important for cell division and the making of blood.

A severe lack of **vitamin B1**, also called **thiamine**, leads to the disease **beriberi**. It damages nerves and the heart. In the past it often occurred where people ate mainly polished white rice. Another example is scurvy, from a lack of vitamin C. In Switzerland, **iodine** has been added to table salt for over a hundred years, to prevent iodine deficiency and goitre.

You can eat enough calories and still get too few micronutrients. This is called **hidden hunger**. It affects very many people around the world, especially where the diet is one-sided. It is best prevented with a **varied diet**: plenty of vegetables, fruit, wholegrain, pulses and, depending on the way you eat, dairy products, fish or meat.

gewusst: Sailors used to get scurvy on long voyages until people noticed that citrus fruits help against it.
In 1922 Switzerland was among the first countries to introduce iodised table salt.

teile.einleitung: Melatonin is a hormone that tells our body that it is night. It is made mainly in the dark and helps to steer the day and night rhythm. It is made chiefly in the pineal gland in the brain.
wichtigste: Melatonin is made mainly in the pineal gland.
The pineal gland looks like a small pine cone.
The melatonin level is highest in the middle of the night.
The body makes melatonin from serotonin.
In old age the production at night usually decreases.
For many animals, melatonin also shows the season.
Melatonin is also found in plants.

abschnitte.text: Melatonin is made mainly in the **pineal gland**. It is only about the size of a pea and lies deep in the brain. It gets its name from its shape: it looks like a small **pine cone**. In German, another word for the stone pine is “Zirbel”, and the gland is named after it. The pineal gland receives information through nerves about whether the eyes are seeing light at that moment or not.

Melatonin was discovered in the 1950s. Researchers found that a substance from the pineal gland **lightens the dark skin of frogs**. It draws together the pigment granules in the skin cells. That is why the hormone was given the name **melatonin**, after the Greek word for “black”. In humans it does not have this effect on skin colour, though.

The body makes melatonin from the messenger substance **serotonin**. When it gets dark, the production rises. The melatonin level is highest **in the middle of the night** and falls again towards morning. Bright light, including from screens, slows the production. In this way melatonin helps to steer the **sleep and wake rhythm**. In **old age**, less melatonin is usually made at night.

In winter the nights are longer, so melatonin is made for longer. In this way melatonin can show many animals the **season**. This helps them, for example, to prepare for hibernation or to change their coat. It is astonishing that melatonin is found **in plants too**. It is found, for example, in cherries, tomatoes and some nuts.

Melatonin does not stay long in the blood. It is broken down mainly in the **liver** and then passed out through the kidneys. That is why the level falls quickly in the morning, when no new melatonin is being made. Melatonin is also available as a medicine, for example against jet lag. In Switzerland it needs a prescription and should only be taken after medical advice.

gewusst: The French philosopher René Descartes thought the pineal gland was the seat of the soul.
Even light at night, for example on a trip to the toilet, can briefly slow the making of melatonin.

teile.einleitung: Measles is an infectious disease caused by a virus. It is one of the most contagious diseases of all. Many people think of it as a harmless childhood illness, but it can be dangerous.
wichtigste: Measles is caused by a virus.
It is very contagious and is passed on through the air.
At the start you often have a fever, a cough and red eyes.
After that a red skin rash appears.
Koplik spots on the lining of the cheek are an early sign.
Usually you get measles at most once in your life.
The Swiss vaccination schedule recommends two doses.

abschnitte.text: Measles is caused by the **measles virus**. It is **very contagious**. When we cough, sneeze or talk, tiny droplets get into the **air**. Anyone who breathes them in can catch it, even if they were only in the same room for a short time. Almost all unprotected people who come into contact with the virus fall ill.

At first you feel as with a bad cold: **fever**, **cough**, a runny nose and **red, inflamed eyes**. An early sign is the **Koplik spots**. These are small whitish spots on the inside of the cheeks. A few days later a **red rash** appears. It usually begins behind the ears and on the face and spreads over the whole body.

Measles weakens the **immune system** for a longer time. That is why other illnesses can follow, such as **pneumonia** or an ear infection. Rare but very dangerous is **inflammation of the brain**. It can leave lasting damage. Even today people around the world still die of measles, above all small children in poorer countries.

Anyone who has had measles once is usually protected for life afterwards. So you get it **at most once**. But it is much safer to be vaccinated. The **Swiss vaccination schedule** recommends **two doses**, usually combined with protection against mumps and rubella. If enough people are vaccinated, the virus can hardly spread any more. This also protects babies who are still too young for the vaccination.

gewusst: After a cough, the measles virus can stay infectious in the air of a room for up to two hours.
Because measles is so contagious, very many people have to be vaccinated so that the disease does not spread.

teile.einleitung: Muscles can become stronger and thicker if you train them. In **muscle building**, training, nutrition and recovery work together. If one of them is missing, the muscle hardly grows.
wichtigste: Through strength training the muscle fibres become thicker, which is called hypertrophy.
Protein is the most important nutrient for muscle building.
The muscles grow mainly in the recovery phase.
Supercompensation means that the body recovers beyond its old level.
Unused muscles waste away, which is called atrophy.
During sleep the body repairs the muscles that have been put under strain.
Humans have about 650 skeletal muscles.

abschnitte.text: Depending on how you count, humans have over 600 **skeletal muscles**, and about **650** is often given. They are fixed to the bones by **tendons**. Tendons transfer the force of the muscle to the bone, while ligaments join bone to bone. Skeletal muscles can be controlled **at will**, and only they are built up in a targeted way with strength training. Heart and smooth muscles work by themselves.

If a muscle is strongly challenged, it adapts. The individual **muscle fibres** become thicker, which is called **hypertrophy**. As a result the muscle becomes bigger and stronger. The opposite is called **atrophy**, the wasting of muscle. Muscles that are not used for weeks, for example because of a plaster cast, become thinner and weaker. With training they can be built up again.

The training only gives the **stimulus**, and growth happens in the **recovery phase**. After a strain the body does not just recover, it even becomes a little more capable than before. This principle is called **supercompensation**. That is why breaks between training sessions are important. Especially valuable is **sleep**: then the body releases growth hormones and repairs the muscles that have been put under strain.

Muscles consist to a large part of **protein**. The body needs it to build new muscle substance after training. Good sources of protein are dairy products, eggs, meat, fish, pulses and nuts. In addition the body needs enough energy from carbohydrates and fat. Anyone who eats a varied diet usually gets enough protein.

gewusst: The largest muscle of the human body is the gluteus maximus.
Children and young people too can safely build up strength with exercises using their own body weight.

teile.einleitung: Even with our eyes closed we know how our arms and legs are lying. The **muscle spindles** help with this. These small sense organs in the muscle measure how long a muscle is at the moment and how quickly it is being stretched.
wichtigste: Muscle spindles measure the length and stretching of the muscle.
Inside them lie intrafusal fibres.
Gamma motor neurons set their sensitivity.
Ia fibres pass on the signals of the primary endings very quickly.
The patellar tendon reflex is based on muscle spindles.
The Golgi tendon organ, on the other hand, measures tension.

abschnitte.text: Muscle spindles are **stretch receptors**. They lie parallel to the normal working fibres in the muscle. If the muscle is stretched, the spindles are stretched too and report this to the spinal cord. In this way the nervous system learns how long a muscle is and how quickly its length is changing. This is important for the **sense of position** and for finely tuned movements.

abschnitte.titel: The structure of a muscle spindle
abschnitte.text: A muscle spindle is surrounded by a capsule. Inside lie special fibres, the **intrafusal fibres**. The normal working fibres outside are called **extrafusal**. According to how their cell nuclei are arranged, two types are told apart. In **nuclear bag fibres** the nuclei are gathered in the middle, and in **nuclear chain fibres** they lie one behind the other in a row. Sensory nerve endings wind around the fibres.

The primary, spirally wound endings are joined to thick, very fast conducting **Ia fibres**. They bring the reports to the spinal cord. The intrafusal fibres are steered by **gamma motor neurons**. These tighten their ends and so set the sensitivity of the spindle. In a voluntary movement **alpha and gamma motor neurons** are activated together. In this way the spindle stays tight even when the muscle shortens and keeps reporting.

If the doctor taps the tendon below the kneecap with a small hammer, the muscle at the front of the thigh is briefly stretched. The spindles report this through Ia fibres to the spinal cord. There the fibre ends directly at the **alpha motor neuron**, which makes the muscle twitch. The leg shoots forwards. Because there is only **one synapse** in between, this **patellar tendon reflex** is especially fast. The **Golgi tendon organ** at the transition from muscle to tendon, on the other hand, mainly measures the tension and reports it through Ib fibres.

gewusst: A reflex like the knee tendon reflex takes place without the brain first thinking about it.
Muscles for fine movements, for example in the hands and neck, contain especially many muscle spindles.

teile.einleitung: Melanocytes are the pigment cells of the skin. They make the pigment melanin and distribute it to the surrounding skin cells. In this way they determine our skin colour and protect against UV radiation.
wichtigste: Melanocytes lie mainly in the stratum basale of the epidermis.
Their precursors come from the neural crest.
Melanin is made in organelles called melanosomes.
The key enzyme is tyrosinase.
Through branched projections they pass the pigment on to keratinocytes.
One melanocyte supplies about 36 keratinocytes.
In vitiligo, melanocytes are lost in sharply bordered patches.

abschnitte.text: The **epidermis**, the outer layer of the skin, consists of several layers. The melanocytes lie mainly in the lowest layer, the **stratum basale**. There they sit between the ordinary skin cells, the **keratinocytes**. Their precursors come from the **neural crest**. This is a tissue from which parts of the nervous system also arise. From there the cells move into the skin even before birth.

Melanocytes make the pigment **melanin** in small sacs, the **melanosomes**. The starting material is the protein building block **tyrosine**. The most important enzyme in this is **tyrosinase**. If it is missing or does not work, no melanin is made. This is the case in one form of **albinism**. Sunlight stimulates the melanocytes to make more melanin.

Melanocytes have long, **branched projections**, like the branches of a tree. Through these projections they pass the melanosomes on to the surrounding **keratinocytes**. One melanocyte supplies about **36 keratinocytes** in this way. In the keratinocytes the melanosomes settle like a **cap** above the cell nucleus. In this way they protect the **DNA**, the genetic information, in particular from UV radiation.

abschnitte.titel: Why skin is different shades of dark
abschnitte.text: People with dark skin do **not have clearly more melanocytes** than people with light skin. What matters is the **amount and kind of melanosomes**. In dark skin they are bigger, more numerous and contain more dark melanin. They are also broken down more slowly in the keratinocytes. This gives a great variety of skin colours.

In **vitiligo**, also called the **white patch disease**, melanocytes are lost in certain areas. **Sharply bordered white patches** appear on the skin. The disease is not contagious and is usually not painful. It is thought that the body’s own immune system attacks the melanocytes. The affected places are especially sensitive to the sun.

gewusst: Melanocytes also sit in the hair roots, and they colour the hair.
The cap of melanin above the cell nucleus works like a little parasol for the genetic information.

teile.einleitung: Macrophages are cells of the immune system. They eat germs, dead cells and foreign bodies. This makes them something like the body’s refuse collection and its guard force at the same time.
wichtigste: Macrophages are made from monocytes, a kind of white blood cell.
The name means “big eater” in Greek.
They recognise bacteria using, among other things, Toll-like receptors.
They kill bacteria they have taken in with reactive oxygen species.
In the spleen they break down old red blood cells.
Alveolar macrophages clean dust from the alveoli.
In tuberculosis they form granulomas around the germs.

abschnitte.text: The word **macrophage** comes from Greek and means **“big eater”**. Macrophages develop from **monocytes**. These are white blood cells that swim in the blood. When they move out of the blood into the tissue, they become macrophages. There they take in foreign material and waste by wrapping themselves around it. This process is called **phagocytosis**.

abschnitte.titel: How they recognise and kill bacteria
abschnitte.text: Macrophages carry special feelers on their surface, the **Toll-like receptors**. With these they recognise typical parts of bacteria, for example the **lipopolysaccharide** from the shell of some bacteria. A bacterium that has been taken in ends up in a sac that fuses with a lysosome. This forms a **phagolysosome**. In it the bacterium is killed and digested using, among other things, **reactive oxygen species**.

Macrophages are found in almost all organs, and they often have names of their own. In the alveoli live the **alveolar macrophages**. They clear away dust particles and germs that have been breathed in. In the **spleen**, macrophages mainly break down old **red blood cells**. In doing so, the iron from the blood pigment is recovered and used again.

Experts roughly distinguish two kinds. **M1 macrophages** promote inflammation and kill bacteria especially effectively. **M2 macrophages** help rather to end inflammation and repair tissue. Macrophages also show other defence cells fragments of the germs. In this way they help to start the targeted defence of the immune system.

Sometimes macrophages also contribute to diseases. In the walls of the blood vessels they can soak up fat. They are then called **foam cells**. They contribute to **arteriosclerosis**, a narrowing of the arteries. In **tuberculosis**, macrophages cannot completely kill the germs. Instead, together with other cells, they wall them off in a little nodule, the **granuloma**.

gewusst: Macrophages in the body break down huge amounts of old red blood cells every day.
The scientist Ilya Mechnikov described the eating cells and received the Nobel Prize in Medicine for it in 1908.

teile.einleitung: Lysosomes are tiny sacs in animal cells. They act like the cell’s digestion and recycling station. With acid enzymes they break down old cell parts and substances that have been taken in.
wichtigste: Lysosomes contain acid hydrolases, enzymes that break down many substances.
Inside, the pH value is about 4.5 to 5.
Proton pumps in the membrane keep the acid conditions going.
In autophagy, the cell breaks down its own damaged parts.
When a phagosome fuses with a lysosome, a phagolysosome forms.
Christian de Duve discovered lysosomes in the 1950s.

abschnitte.text: A **lysosome** is a small sac surrounded by a membrane. Inside it there is an **acid pH value** of about **4.5 to 5**, clearly more acid than in the rest of the inside of the cell. **Proton pumps** in the membrane see to this. They constantly pump hydrogen ions into the lysosome. Lysosomes contain numerous enzymes, the **acid hydrolases**. They can break down proteins, fats, sugars and genetic material.

Lysosomes break down substances that the cell has taken in from outside. When an eating cell eats a bacterium, for example, it first lies in a sac, the **phagosome**. When this fuses with a lysosome, a **phagolysosome** forms, in which the bacterium is digested. In **autophagy** the cell breaks down its **own damaged parts**. It can use the building blocks again.

Lysosomal enzymes are dangerous, because they could digest the cell itself. But if they get into the **cytoplasm**, they usually do only little damage. The reason: there the pH value is **neutral**, and at a neutral pH these enzymes are **hardly active**. This is how the cell protects itself from its own tools.

The Belgian scientist **Christian de Duve** discovered lysosomes in the **1950s**. For this he received the Nobel Prize in Medicine in 1974 together with others. If a single lysosomal enzyme is missing or **faulty**, undigested substances build up in the cell. This gives rise to **lysosomal storage diseases** such as **Tay-Sachs disease**. They are rare and usually inherited.

gewusst: The name “lysosome” comes from Greek and means roughly “dissolving body”.
A Nobel Prize was awarded in 2016 for research on autophagy.

teile.einleitung: **Graves’ disease**, in German called Morbus Basedow, is a disease of the thyroid gland. The body’s own immune system constantly drives the thyroid on, so that it makes too many hormones. This is called an overactive thyroid.
wichtigste: Graves’ disease is an autoimmune disease of the thyroid gland.
Autoantibodies stimulate the TSH receptor and cause an overactive thyroid.
The Merseburg triad consists of a goitre, bulging eyes and a racing heart.
In English the disease is named after Robert Graves, and in German after Carl von Basedow.
The TSH value is strongly lowered in an overactive thyroid.
It is treated with thiamazole, radioiodine therapy or an operation.

abschnitte.text: The **thyroid gland** lies at the front of the neck and makes hormones that steer the metabolism. Normally the pituitary gland gives the signal for this with the hormone **TSH**. In Graves’ disease the immune system makes **autoantibodies** that stimulate the TSH receptor. They imitate TSH and constantly drive the thyroid on. The many thyroid hormones inhibit the pituitary gland, so the **TSH value is strongly lowered**. The antibodies still drive the gland on.

In an overactive thyroid the **metabolism runs at full speed**. People affected often lose weight although they have a good appetite. Restlessness, sweating, trembling and a fast pulse are added. The doctor **Carl von Basedow** from Merseburg described three typical signs in 1840: an enlarged thyroid (**goitre**), bulging eyes (**exophthalmos**) and a racing heart. They are called the **Merseburg triad**. Not all sick people show all three signs.

In some people affected, the eyes are also involved. This **endocrine orbitopathy** arises because tissue and muscles behind the eye swell and push it forwards. The eyes can then be red, dry or sensitive to light. **Smoking** makes the involvement of the eyes clearly worse.

Medicines such as **thiamazole** belong to the antithyroid drugs. They inhibit the building of iodine into the thyroid hormones, so the production of hormones falls. In **radioiodine therapy**, the thyroid takes up radioactive iodine-131 and is irradiated from the inside. This ends the overactivity for good. Another possibility is an **operation** in which the thyroid is removed wholly or in part.

gewusst: The Irish doctor Robert Graves described the disease as early as 1835, which is why it is called Graves’ disease in English.
The thyroid gland needs iodine to make its hormones.

teile.einleitung: **Crohn’s disease** is a chronic, that is, long-lasting, inflammation in the digestive tract. It comes in flare-ups and can affect any section from the mouth to the anus. Together with ulcerative colitis it belongs to the chronic inflammatory bowel diseases.
wichtigste: Crohn’s disease can affect the whole digestive tract from the mouth to the anus.
Most often affected is the terminal ileum, the end of the small intestine.
Healthy and inflamed sections alternate.
The inflammation reaches through all layers of the intestinal wall.
Typical complications are fistulas.
Smoking clearly raises the risk and the severity.
The disease is named after Burrill B. Crohn.

abschnitte.text: In **Crohn’s disease** the digestive tract is inflamed again and again. The disease usually runs in **flare-ups**, between which there are calmer times. Typical complaints are stomach pain, diarrhoea, tiredness and loss of weight. Crohn’s disease is not contagious. The exact causes are not yet fully understood, and a combination of genes, the immune system, gut bacteria and the environment is suspected.

Crohn’s disease can affect **any section** of the digestive tract, from the mouth to the anus. Most often it is the **terminal ileum** that is affected, the transition from the small intestine to the large intestine. That is why the disease used to be called ileitis terminalis too. Typical is **discontinuous** involvement: inflamed sections alternate with healthy ones, which is called skip lesions. **Ulcerative colitis**, on the other hand, is confined to the large intestine and spreads continuously.

The inflammation is **transmural**, which means it affects all layers of the intestinal wall. As a result it can bore through the wall and form passages to other organs or to the skin. Such passages are called **fistulas**, and they often occur around the anus. Collections of pus and narrowings of the intestine can also arise. Under the microscope one often finds **granulomas without caseation**, small nodules of defence cells.

**Smoking** raises the risk and leads to more severe courses, so stopping smoking is part of the treatment. In 2001 the gene **NOD2** was described as the first genetic risk factor. NOD2 helps the defence system to recognise parts of bacteria. The disease is named after the American doctor **Burrill B. Crohn**, who described it in 1932 with colleagues. So far Crohn’s disease cannot be cured, but medicines can calm the inflammation well.

gewusst: Crohn’s disease often begins as early as in the teenage years or as a young adult.
In Switzerland, a large research study has for years followed people with chronic inflammatory bowel diseases.

teile.einleitung: On almost every food packet there is a date. The **best-before date** says until when a product safely keeps its quality. But it is not an expiry date after which you have to throw everything away.
wichtigste: The best-before date is the date until which a product keeps its quality.
On the packet it usually says “best before”.
Until this date the manufacturer guarantees the quality.
The date applies only to the unopened packet that has been stored correctly.
Foods that spoil easily carry “use by” instead.
After the best-before date you check a product by looking, smelling and tasting.
Table salt normally carries no best-before date.

abschnitte.text: The **best-before date** is a promise from the manufacturer. Until this day the food keeps its qualities such as taste, smell, colour and nutritional value. On the packet it usually says “best before” with the date. Important: the date applies only to the **unopened packet** that is stored correctly, for example cool or dry. After opening, a product can spoil more quickly.

For foods that spoil easily, such as minced meat, fresh poultry or raw fish, there is a different statement: **“use by”**. This is the use-by date. After this day you should no longer eat the product, even if it still looks good. This is because **dangerous germs** may have formed that you can neither see nor smell. These two statements are also used in Switzerland.

When the best-before date has passed, a food is often still edible. You check it with your senses: **look, smell and taste**. A yoghurt that looks normal, smells normal and tastes normal can usually still be eaten. If the lid is bulging, it smells strange or mould shows, it belongs in the bin. Anyone who goes about it like this throws away less food unnecessarily.

abschnitte.titel: What keeps for a long time
abschnitte.text: Dry foods such as **pasta**, rice or sugar often keep long beyond the date if stored dry. Fresh meat, fish and raw milk, on the other hand, spoil quickly. Some foods need no best-before date at all, for example **table salt**, because it practically does not spoil. Fresh fruit and vegetables also usually carry none.

gewusst: A large part of the food that is thrown away would still be edible, and products often end up in the bin because of a passed best-before date.
Sugar and salt hardly ever spoil, because germs find hardly any water in them to live on.

teile.einleitung: Lymph is a pale liquid that flows through the body in vessels of its own. It collects surplus tissue fluid and brings it back into the blood. On the way it is filtered in the lymph nodes.
wichtigste: Lymph is a pale liquid in the lymph vessels.
It is made from tissue fluid.
At the end it flows into the venous blood near the heart.
Lymph nodes filter the lymph and fight off germs.
Lymph contains particularly many lymphocytes.
In the intestine, lymph takes up fats in particular.

abschnitte.text: A little liquid constantly leaks out of the finest blood vessels into the tissue. It supplies the cells. Most of it returns to the blood, but a remainder stays in the tissue. This **tissue fluid** is taken up by fine **lymph vessels** and is then called **lymph**. It is pale, usually almost transparent. Without lymph vessels the tissue would swell.

The lymph vessels join up into ever larger channels. The largest lymph channel in the body is called the **thoracic duct**. At the end the lymph flows **into the venous blood near the heart**. Lymph has no heart of its own to pump it. It is driven along mainly by the **movements of the muscles around it**. Little valves make sure that it does not flow backwards.

On its way the lymph flows through many **lymph nodes**. These **filter** the lymph and **fight off germs**. Lymph contains particularly many **lymphocytes**, a kind of white blood cell. In a **sore throat** the lymph nodes in the neck often swell, because they are fighting the germs there.

In the intestine, lymph has a special job. It takes up **fats** from food in particular. After a meal rich in fat, the lymph from the intestine therefore looks milky white. This is how the thoracic duct got its German name, the “milk-chest duct”. Through it the fats finally reach the blood.

gewusst: Several litres of lymph flow through the body every day.
Movement helps lymph to flow, which is why legs swell more easily when you sit still for a long time.
